pages.explain: In 1971, at an unofficial women's World Cup, Argentina's women beat England 4–1 at the Azteca.

pages.text: **Elba Selva** scored all four goals that day. August 21 is now the **Día de la Futbolista**, the Day of the Woman Footballer.

classes.title: Messi and Qatar
classes.summary: Heartbreak in Brazil, glory in Qatar, one more final in 2026

pages.text: **Messi** grew up in Rosario and left for Barcelona at 13. For years, some Argentines complained that he only played well for Barça.

pages.prompt: Why did Messi move to Barcelona as a kid?
options: Barça paid for his growth treatment
His dad got a job in Spain
He won a TV talent contest
pages.explain: He needed growth-hormone treatment his family couldn't afford. Barcelona paid for it.

pages.text: 2014 World Cup final, in Brazil: Germany scores in extra time. Messi walks past the trophy he couldn't touch. That photo still hurts.

After more lost finals, Messi quit the national team in 2016. Half the country begged him to come back. He did, and in 2021 he finally won a title with Argentina: the Copa América, against Brazil, in the Maracanã.
Qatar 2022, the final against France: 2–0, 2–2, 3–2, 3–3. Then penalties. **Dibu Martínez** saves one, **Montiel** scores the last. Messi finally lifts the cup.

pages.prompt: How many people filled Buenos Aires to welcome the team home?
pages.explain: Millions. The team bus couldn't get through, and the players finished the parade by helicopter.

pages.text: The soundtrack of Qatar: **“Muchachos, ahora nos volvimos a ilusionar”**, a fan chant sung to a song by La Mosca. Start it at any party and the whole room joins in.
In 2026 the team, known as **la Scaloneta** after coach Scaloni, reached the final again and lost 1–0 to Spain in extra time. Weeks later, Messi retired from the national team.

classes.title: Beyond Buenos Aires
classes.summary: Rosario, Córdoba and La Plata, where the local derby matters more than Boca–River

pages.text: In cities with their own big clubs, like Rosario, Córdoba or La Plata, the local **clásico** matters more than Boca–River. Ask someone from Rosario about Newell's and Central, and you'll be listening for an hour.

pages.prompt: Newell's fans proudly call themselves **leprosos**, an old word for people with leprosy. Where does that come from?
options: They agreed to a charity match for people with leprosy
Their first stadium was an old hospital
pages.explain: The story goes: around 1920, both Rosario clubs were invited to play a charity match for people with leprosy. Newell's said yes. Off the pitch, the word is offensive.

pages.text: Legend says Rosario Central turned that match down, so they became the **canallas**: the scoundrels. Nobody can prove it, and both clubs wear the insults with pride.
Even the Selección splits: **Messi** grew up a Newell's kid, **Di María** is pure Central.

In La Plata it's **Estudiantes** against **Gimnasia**. Estudiantes fans are **pinchas**, short for **pincharratas** (rat-stabbers), Gimnasia fans are **triperos**. In Córdoba, it's **Belgrano** against **Talleres**.

pages.prompt: Gimnasia fans are called **triperos**, tripe people. Why?
options: Many early fans worked in meatpacking plants
They grill tripe outside every match
Their old shirt looked like tripe
pages.explain: The meatpacking plants near La Plata employed thousands. Their workers followed Gimnasia.

sections.title: How Argentines are
sections.summary: The ego, the drama and the complaints, as Argentines tell it themselves

classes.title: The famous ego
classes.summary: The joke all of Latin America tells, and Argentines tell first

pages.text: Ask anyone in Latin America about Argentines and you'll hear one word: **ego**. Argentines, people say, think they are the best. Argentines know the jokes, and tell them first.

pages.prompt: A joke from the rest of Latin America starts: “What is the ego?” How does it end?
options: “The little Argentine we all have inside”
pages.explain: **“El pequeño argentino que todos llevamos dentro.”** Another one: in a storm, an Argentine looks up at the lightning and smiles. He thinks God is taking his photo.

pages.text: The proof they give, as a joke: the Pope was Argentine, Messi and Maradona are Argentine, even the queen of the Netherlands is Argentine. So, they say, **Dios es argentino**.
In the provinces, people say the ego lives in Buenos Aires. Their word for it is **agrandado**. The cure is a friend who says **“bajá un cambio”**: calm down.

pages.prompt: Argentines say they have the best meat, the best fans and the best ice cream in the world. And when the news is bad, like prices going up fast?
pages.explain: Never in the middle, the joke goes: the best football and the worst economy, the best friends and the worst traffic. Being a normal country would be the real insult.

pages.text: Uruguayans have their own complaint: Argentines, they say, think that [mate], tango, [dulce de leche] and the [asado] are all Argentine. Uruguay says every one of them is Uruguayan too.
The soft side: the people with the famous ego are also the first to laugh at it. Nobody tells more jokes about Argentines than Argentines.

classes.title: Complaining, with love
classes.summary: The national sport that is not football

pages.text: Argentines say complaining is their national sport. Two words start it: **“Este país…”** This country… Then comes a long breath, and everybody at the table agrees.

pages.prompt: A classic line from someone who is tired of it all: “The only way out is…” What?
pages.explain: **“La única salida es Ezeiza”**: the international airport of Buenos Aires. Many people say it. Few buy the ticket.

pages.text: The list is always the same: prices, politicians, traffic, the bank, the heat. Ask **“¿Todo bien?”** in a line at the shop and you can hear all five before your turn.
Another favorite: **“Argentina no es para principiantes.”** Argentina is not for beginners. It's a complaint and a little pride at the same time.

pages.prompt: Your Argentine friend says the country is a disaster. You, a foreigner, say he's right. What happens?
options: He thanks you for being honest
pages.explain: Only Argentines can speak badly of Argentina. From you, he wants to hear about the meat, the people and Messi.

pages.text: And the same person who complained all through dinner will tell you at dessert that he could never live in any other country.
You can complain too, about small things. **“¡Qué caro está todo!”** Everything is so expensive! Everyone agrees, and you have new friends.

classes.title: Everyone is an expert
classes.summary: Opinions on everything, all at the same time

pages.text: Argentines joke that they have an opinion about everything, and share it. Someone who gives opinions on every subject, knowing or not, is an **opinólogo**.

pages.prompt: Four friends sit in a café for three hours and solve every problem of the country. What do Argentines call that?
pages.explain: **Arreglar el mundo**: to fix the world. Nothing changes outside the café, but everyone goes home feeling better.

pages.text: The classic expert is the taxi driver. In ten blocks he explains how to fix the economy, the national team and your love life, and he doesn't charge extra.
The classic start: **“¿Sabés cuál es el problema de este país?”** Do you know what this country's problem is? Don't answer. The speaker already has the answer, and it's long.

pages.prompt: Two friends shout at each other about politics for an hour at dinner. How does the night end?
options: They don't speak for a month
They hug and plan the next dinner
pages.explain: Arguing is a way of spending time together. A loud **discusión**, an argument, is not a fight. Between friends, silence would be worse.

pages.text: Still, some subjects are too dangerous. Many families have one rule for Sunday lunch: no politics at the table. It lasts until the coffee.
To give your opinion, don't wait for silence. Say **“para mí…”**, for me…, and go. And when you agree with someone: **“Tal cual.”** Exactly.

classes.title: A little drama
classes.summary: Big words for small things, and feelings in public

pages.text: Argentines say of themselves that they exaggerate. Nothing is just good or bad. It's **lo más**, the best thing ever, or **un desastre**, a disaster.

pages.prompt: Your friend arrives and says **“me quiero morir”**: I want to die. What probably happened?
options: She left her phone charger at home
Someone in her family is very sick
pages.explain: Small problems get big words. **“Me muero”**, I'm dying, can be about hunger, heat, laughing or shame. When something is really serious, people speak more quietly.

pages.text: Every story starts the same way: **“No sabés lo que me pasó.”** You have no idea what happened to me. What happened: the bus was late.
Feelings are shown. A man can cry in public for a goal, a song or a goodbye, and nobody finds it strange.

pages.prompt: A young man is leaving to work abroad for one year. Who comes to the airport to say goodbye?
options: Nobody: goodbyes are said at home
pages.explain: Ten or fifteen people, tears and a long group hug. Coming back is the same, with a sign that says **“Bienvenido”**: welcome.

pages.text: One Argentine word is hard to translate: **histeriquear**. You show interest in someone, then you go cold, again and again. People accuse each other of it all the time.
Argentines joke that this is why Buenos Aires is so full of psychologists. Going to therapy is normal, and people talk about it at dinner.

classes.title: Argentines abroad
classes.summary: How to find one anywhere in the world

pages.text: Many Argentines go to live abroad, above all in Spain. It's easier for them than for most: a grandparent from Italy or Spain often means a European passport.

pages.prompt: On a beach on the other side of the world, how do two Argentines find each other?
options: By the mate and the termo
pages.explain: A termo, the bottle of hot water for mate, works like a flag. (It could be a Uruguayan. They ask anyway.) Then comes **“¿De dónde sos?”** Where are you from? Ten minutes later they have friends in common.

pages.text: The suitcase of an Argentine abroad carries [yerba], [dulce de leche] and alfajores. And anyone who visits from home gets a shopping list first.
They look for each other. In every big city there's an Argentine bakery, a group that plays football on Sundays and someone making an [asado] on a very small balcony.

pages.prompt: A plane from Europe lands in Buenos Aires. What do many passengers do?
options: They call home before the doors open
pages.explain: Clapping when the plane lands is a habit Argentines are famous for. Some people find it embarrassing, and clap anyway.

pages.text: What they feel has a verb: **extrañar**, to miss. **“Extraño el asado, a mis amigos, los domingos.”** Nobody says they miss the prices.
At the World Cup in Qatar, tens of thousands of Argentine fans made every game feel like a home game. Some sold their car to pay for the trip.

classes.title: Getting through it
classes.summary: A country of crises, and people proud of surviving them

pages.text: Argentines have lived through many crises: prices that double, savings that disappear, rules that change in one night. People say there's one every ten years.

pages.prompt: A famous economist is said to have joked that there are four kinds of countries: rich, poor, Japan and… which one?
pages.explain: Japan, because nobody understood how it became rich so fast. Argentina, because nobody understood how such a rich country became poorer. Argentines love to repeat it.

pages.text: A very Argentine verb is **zafar**: to get out of a problem at the last second. **“Zafé”** means: that was close, but I'm fine.
A small extra way to make money is a **rebusque**: selling cakes, driving at night, fixing phones. Many people have one, and they are proud of knowing how to invent it.

pages.prompt: When prices rise fast, what do many Argentines do with their salary on the day it arrives?
options: Leave it in the bank for months
Spend it or change it fast
pages.explain: Pesos lose value, so people fill the fridge, pay their monthly payments or buy dollars the same week. Saving in pesos feels like losing money.

pages.text: So people enjoy today. In the middle of a crisis, on a Tuesday night, the pizzerías are full. Visitors never understand it.
The pride is this: **“De esta también salimos.”** We'll get through this one too. And while it's still happening, someone is already making jokes about it.

sections.title: Family and friends
sections.summary: Sunday lunch, nicknames, love and parties until sunrise

classes.title: Sunday is for family
classes.summary: A lunch that ends at night, and a tupper to take home

pages.text: Sunday lunch belongs to the family. Everyone goes to the parents' or grandparents' house, for pasta or an [asado]. It starts around two and ends when it's dark.
Families are close. Cousins, **primos**, grow up almost like brothers and sisters. And kids call their parents' best friends **tío** and **tía**: uncle and aunt.

pages.prompt: At what age do many Argentines leave their parents' home?
options: In their late twenties, or later
pages.explain: Rent is expensive, and most people study at a university in their own city while living at home. Nobody thinks it's strange.

pages.text: Grandparents are **abuelo** and **abuela**, or just **abu**. In Italian families, **nono** and **nona**. In Jewish families, **zeide** and **bobe**.
You don't leave with empty hands. Mom or grandma fills a **tupper**, a plastic box, with what's left of lunch. The rule: the [tupper] comes back.

pages.prompt: After a lunch like that, what do many families do for dinner on Sunday night?
pages.explain: Nobody wants to cook again. Sunday night is the big night for pizza and empanadas delivered to your door.

pages.text: Invited to a family lunch? Bring dessert or a bottle of wine, kiss everyone hello, grandma too, and say yes when they offer you more food.

classes.title: Nobody uses your real name
classes.summary: Pancho, el Colo, la Negra and the waiter who calls you boss

pages.text: A nickname is an **apodo**, and almost everyone has one. Some come with the name: Francisco is **Pancho**, José is **Pepe**, Ignacio is **Nacho**, Dolores is **Lola**.
Other names are just cut short: **Fede**, **Mati**, **Sofi**, **Cami**, **Juli**, **Nico**, **Santi**. If your name is long, people will cut it in half.

pages.prompt: A friend says: “This is **el Colo**.” What does [el Colo] look like?
pages.explain: From **colorado**, red. Looks become names: **Flaco** (thin), **Gordo** (fat), **Negra** (dark hair or skin), **Rulo** (curly). Between friends it's love. As a foreigner, don't copy it.

pages.text: Friends get new names from one funny moment. Fall asleep at one party, and you can be **el Dormido**, the sleeping one, for the next twenty years.

pages.prompt: A waiter you've never seen calls you **jefe**, boss. Why?
options: He thinks you're the one who pays
It's a friendly way to talk to a stranger
pages.explain: Men call strangers **jefe**, **maestro** or **campeón**: boss, master, champion. It's warm, not serious. And a nice person is a **genio** or a **genia**.

pages.text: Someone with the same name as you is your **tocayo** or **tocaya**. Two Martíns meet, and one says **“¡Tocayo!”** It's a small instant friendship.
Family nicknames last for life. A man of seventy can still be **el Nene**, the kid, and many people don't know their neighbor Cacho's real name.

classes.title: Friends are family
classes.summary: The same group for thirty years, and how friends look after each other

pages.text: Friends are a second family. Many people keep the same group from school for life: **los chicos del colegio**, still together at forty, fifty and sixty.

pages.prompt: A group of friends from school, now forty years old. What do they do every Thursday night?
pages.explain: **El asado de los jueves**, the Thursday barbecue. Or **fútbol 5**, with five players per team, on Tuesdays, then pizza. The day is fixed and nobody books anything else.

pages.text: The verb is **juntarse**: to get together. **“¿Nos juntamos?”** needs no plan and no reason. And **“Caete por casa”** means: come over, any time.
Friends say **te quiero**, I love you, to each other. Men too, with a long hug. Nobody finds it strange.

pages.prompt: You lost your job and you feel terrible. What does a real friend say?
pages.explain: **Bancar** a friend is to be with them when things go wrong. **“Te banco”**: I'm with you, whatever happens. (Bancar can also mean to wait, or to put up with something.)

pages.text: When a friend moves abroad, there is a **despedida**: a goodbye party, usually an [asado], with speeches and tears. Some people get three or four of them.
Say yes to the first invitation, even if it starts at eleven at night. Soon someone adds you to the **grupo de WhatsApp**, and that's how you know you're one of them.

classes.title: Love and dating
classes.summary: The steps of a couple, the message with no answer and the big Sunday test

pages.text: The steps: first you're **saliendo**, going out. Then you're **de novios**, an official couple. Then comes **convivir**, living together. Many couples never marry at all.
Before all that there is the **casi algo**, the “almost something”: you see each other, you write every day, and nobody says what it is.

pages.prompt: Your friend wrote to the boy she likes. He read the message at nine. It's midnight and there's no answer. What does she tell the group?
pages.explain: **El visto** is the mark that shows a message was seen. **Clavar el visto** is to see it and say nothing. Her friends will study it with her for hours.

pages.text: The real test is the family. When your partner invites you to Sunday lunch with parents, grandparents and cousins, it's serious. Everyone will ask you questions.
**Novio** and **novia** have no age limit: a woman of sixty can introduce her **novio**. A neutral word for any partner is **pareja**.

pages.prompt: In 2010 Argentina became the first country in Latin America to do something. What?
options: Allow marriage between two men or two women
Give fathers a month off for a new baby
pages.explain: The law is called **matrimonio igualitario**, equal marriage. It was a fast change: the divorce law is only from 1987.

pages.text: Young couples celebrate every month together, not only every year: **“Cumplimos seis meses.”** We've been together six months.
Many people live with their parents until almost thirty. So couples go to a **telo**, a hotel with rooms by the hour. It's normal, and nobody is embarrassed.

classes.title: Weddings and fifteenth birthdays
classes.summary: The two biggest parties in a family, and what to give

pages.text: A wedding is a **casamiento**. Only the one at the public office counts by law: **el civil**. Outside, friends throw rice. The big party often comes days later.

pages.prompt: The wedding party starts at nine at night. When does it end?
options: Around five or six in the morning
pages.explain: A party that ends at two is a bad party. Grandparents stay until four. The last thing served is breakfast: coffee and medialunas, small sweet croissants.

pages.text: Dinner comes in parts, and between them everyone gets up to dance. Each block of dancing is a **tanda**. So you eat, dance, eat, dance.
Late at night comes the **carnaval carioca**. Staff hand out funny hats, masks, whistles and foam, called **cotillón**, and the music gets fast and loud.
Then the **mesa dulce** opens: a long table full of cakes and sweets, after midnight, for people who thought they could not eat more.

pages.prompt: A girl's 15th birthday is the **fiesta de quince**, as big as a wedding. Who dances the first waltz with her?
pages.explain: Then the grandfathers, uncles and friends take turns. Today many girls ask for a trip with friends instead of the party.

pages.text: What to give at a wedding? Money is normal. Many invitations come with the couple's bank details, and nobody thinks that's rude.

sections.title: Home
sections.summary: Flats, neighbors and the shops on your block

classes.title: A flat with two ambientes
classes.summary: How homes are counted, numbered and kept dark

pages.text: Flats are not counted by bedrooms. They are counted in **ambientes**: rooms, and the living room is one of them. A **dos ambientes** is one bedroom and one living room.

pages.prompt: The smallest flat has one room where you sleep, eat and live. What is it called in an ad?
pages.explain: A **monoambiente**: one single room. The kitchen and the bathroom are never counted. (**Medio ambiente** means the environment, as in nature.)

pages.text: An address looks like this: **4° B**. Fourth floor, flat B. **PB** is the **planta baja**, the ground floor. So the first floor is one floor up from the street.
A **PH** is a flat inside an old, low house. No lift, but often a patio or a terrace of its own, and almost no monthly building fees. People love them.

pages.prompt: Next to the toilet there is a second, low bowl with its own taps. What is it for?
options: Washing your feet after the beach
Washing yourself after using the toilet
pages.explain: It's the **bidet**, and almost every bathroom in Argentina has one. Argentines who move abroad say it's one of the things they miss most.

pages.text: Windows have **persianas**: heavy shutters that roll down on the outside. Pull them all the way down and the room is completely dark, even at noon.
Two words to look for in an ad. **Al frente**: windows on the street, with light and bus noise. **Contrafrente**: at the back, darker but quiet.

classes.title: The encargado
classes.summary: The person who runs your building, and the neighbors' meetings

pages.text: Most buildings have an **encargado**. He or she cleans, takes out the rubbish, receives your parcels and knows everything about everyone. Many of them live in the building.

pages.prompt: Besides rent, what else do you pay every month in a building?
options: A tax on people who rent
Your share of the building's costs
pages.explain: They're called **expensas**: the encargado's salary, the lift, the cleaning, the lights in the hall. Expensas can be high, so always ask **“¿Cuánto son las expensas?”** before you rent.

pages.text: All the owners together are the **consorcio**. Their meetings are famous: three hours of arguing about the lift, the noise and whose bike is in the hall.
The intercom at the street door is the **portero eléctrico**. A friend rings and says **“¡Soy yo!”** It's me. Nobody says their name.

pages.prompt: Your friend rings from the street at night. In many buildings, what do you have to do?
options: Go down and open the door with your key
Press a button in your flat
pages.explain: For safety, many street doors only open with a key. So the answer to the intercom is **“¡Bajo!”**: I'm coming down.

pages.text: In the lift, you say hello and goodbye to strangers. **“Buen día”** when you get in, **“hasta luego”** when you get out. Saying nothing is rude.
Old lifts have two metal doors that you close by hand. If one is left open, the lift can't move, and someone on another floor shouts **“¡Ascensor!”**

classes.title: The shops on your block
classes.summary: Small shops, how to ask, and what you get for free

pages.text: Many Argentines still buy food in small shops near home: the **verdulería** for fruit and vegetables, the **carnicería** for meat, the **panadería** for bread.

pages.prompt: It's ten at night and you need milk. Which shop on the block is probably still open?
pages.explain: People call it **el chino**, because many are run by families who came from China. It's an everyday name, not an insult. **“Voy al chino”**: I'm going to the shop.

pages.text: At the **fiambrería** you buy ham and cheese by weight, and you only say the number: **“cien de jamón, doscientos de queso”**. A hundred grams of ham, two hundred of cheese.
At the [verdulería] you usually don't choose the fruit yourself. You say what you want and when you'll eat it: **“para hoy”**, for today, means give me the ripe ones.

pages.prompt: By old custom, what does the verdulero add to your bag for free?
pages.explain: **Perejil**, parsley. You just ask **“¿me das un poco de perejil?”** With prices going up, some shops now charge for it, and people complain about that.

pages.text: The **dietética** sells nuts, seeds, flour and spices from big open bags, by weight. Every barrio has a few now.
Every shop ends the same way. They ask **“¿Algo más?”** Anything else? You say **“Nada más, gracias. ¿Cuánto es?”**

sections.title: Everyday life
sections.summary: The weather, the doctor and the road

classes.title: Talking about the weather
classes.summary: What people say in the lift, and the storms with names

pages.text: The seasons are the other way round. Summer is December to March, and the cold months are June, July and August.

pages.prompt: It's 30 °C in Buenos Aires and everyone feels terrible. What does every porteño say?
options: “It's not the heat that kills you, it's the humidity”
pages.explain: **“Lo que mata es la humedad.”** It's said so often that it's a joke by now. A hot, wet, heavy day is **pesado**.

pages.text: The weather report gives two numbers: the real temperature and the **sensación térmica**, how it feels on your skin. People only repeat the second one.
In a January heat wave, every air conditioner is on and whole barrios lose power. **“Se cortó la luz”**, the power went out, is a classic summer phrase.
Around August 30 comes the **tormenta de Santa Rosa**, a big storm named after the saint of that day. People wait for it, and the news reports if it came or not.

pages.prompt: Has it ever snowed in the city of Buenos Aires?
pages.explain: On July 9, 2007 the city turned white for the first time since 1918. People ran out to touch it. Everyone remembers where they were that day.

pages.text: A **sudestada** is a strong wind from the southeast with days of rain. It pushes the river up, and the low barrios near the water get flooded.
The weather starts every chat in a lift. **“¡Qué calor!”** How hot! **“¡Qué frío!”** How cold! **“Refrescó”**: it got cooler.

classes.title: Seeing a doctor
classes.summary: The guardia, the green cross and three ways to be covered

pages.text: Public hospitals are free for Argentines and permanent residents, and an emergency is free for anyone. They can be slow and crowded, but many of the best doctors work there.

pages.prompt: You feel very bad at two in the morning. Where do you go?
options: To the guardia of a hospital
You wait and call a doctor at eight
pages.explain: The **guardia** is the part of a hospital that takes people without an appointment, day and night. For an ambulance, call **107**.

pages.text: There are three ways to be covered: the public hospital, an **obra social** (health cover that comes with your job) or a **prepaga** (a private plan you pay every month).
A pharmacy has a green cross. At night and on Sundays one pharmacy in each area stays open: the **farmacia de turno**. The list is on the door of every closed one.

pages.prompt: Besides selling medicine, what can many pharmacies do for you?
pages.explain: You buy the medicine and they give you the injection in a small room at the back. Many also take your blood pressure.

pages.text: To see a doctor you need a **turno**, an appointment. And at any desk you may hear **“se cayó el sistema”**: the computers stopped. Everyone waits; nobody is surprised.
What to say: **“Me duele la cabeza”**, my head hurts. **“Tengo fiebre”**, I have a fever. **“Estoy resfriado”** (or **resfriada**), I have a cold.
Tens of thousands of foreigners study medicine in Argentina, and more than half of them come from Brazil. In some classrooms you hear a lot of Portuguese.

classes.title: On the road
classes.summary: Long roads, service stations and parking in the city

pages.text: The country is huge. Buenos Aires to Bariloche is about 1,600 km, close to twenty hours by car. Families do it anyway, with a [termo] and a [mate].

pages.prompt: On a road between cities, what must every driver do by law, even at noon on a sunny day?
pages.explain: Low lights on, day and night, on every **ruta**. A ruta is a road between towns; inside the city it's a street or an avenue.

pages.text: You don't fill the tank yourself. At the **estación de servicio** a worker does it. Gas for the car is **nafta**, and you say **“Llenalo, por favor”**: fill it up.

pages.prompt: Many service stations have a machine made just for travelers. What does it give?
pages.explain: For a small price, or free, it fills your thermos with water at the right temperature. Every road trip stops for it.

pages.text: Park near a stadium or a concert and a man waves a cloth to guide you in. He is a **trapito**, and he expects a tip to “look after” your car.
A car stopped in the second lane with its warning lights on is in **doble fila**. Those lights are the **balizas**, and they mean: “I'm coming back in a minute.”
Words for the car: **el auto**, **el baúl** (the trunk), **la goma** (the tire), **estacionar** (to park). A flat tire: **“Pinché una goma.”**

sections.title: Drinks
sections.summary: Wine with ice, one beer for the whole table, fernet and vermut

classes.title: Wine, the easy way
classes.summary: How wine is really drunk at a family table, and how to toast

pages.text: Wine is **vino**, and at a normal table it's red: **vino tinto**. Nobody smells it or talks about it for ten minutes. You pour and you eat.

pages.prompt: It's a hot day at a family [asado]. What do many people put in their glass of red wine?
pages.explain: Wine with **soda** and **hielo**, ice. In an expensive restaurant people may look at you. At a family table it's the normal thing in summer.

pages.text: The grape that made Argentina famous is **Malbec**. In the dry sun and high land of Mendoza it gives a dark, soft red wine.
Since 2013, wine is Argentina's national drink by law. [Mate] has a different title: the national infusion.

pages.prompt: In old neighborhood restaurants, house wine comes to the table in a ceramic jug. What shape is the jug?
pages.explain: It's the **pingüino**, and the wine comes out of its beak. Nobody is sure why a penguin. Today people buy them as presents.

pages.text: For a big party, wine is bought in a **damajuana**: a round glass bottle of five liters with a handle, often in a basket.
To toast, lift your glass and say **“¡Salud!”** Look the other person in the eyes. And don't toast with water: people say it brings bad luck.

classes.title: One beer, many glasses
classes.summary: How to order it, share it and buy it at the kiosco

pages.text: Beer is **cerveza**, and between friends it's **birra**, from Italian. **“¿Tomamos una birra?”** is an invitation to talk, more than to drink.

pages.prompt: Four friends sit down at a bar and order beer. What usually comes to the table?
options: One big bottle and four glasses
One very big glass with four straws
pages.explain: The classic size is the liter bottle, and it's for sharing. You fill the others' glasses before your own.

pages.text: The classic brand is **Quilmes**, with the colors of the flag on its label. It was born in 1888 in the city of Quilmes, just south of Buenos Aires.
A small bottle for one person is a **porrón**. Beer from the tap is **tirada**, and a tall glass of it is a **pinta**, from the English *pint*.

pages.prompt: You want to buy a liter of beer at the [kiosco] and the seller asks **“¿Tenés envase?”** What does he want?
options: Your ID, to see your age
pages.explain: The glass bottle, the **envase**, is used again and again. You bring an empty one or you pay extra. That's why homes keep empty bottles by the door.

pages.text: In the last ten years, small breweries opened in every barrio, selling their own beer: **cerveza artesanal**. The early evening, when it's cheaper, is the *happy hour*, said in English.
The usual thing to eat with it is a **picada**: a board of cheese, salami, olives and bread in the middle of the table. Everyone picks from it with their hands.

classes.title: Fernet and vermut
classes.summary: A bitter black drink for parties, and an old custom that came back

pages.text: **Fernet** is a black, bitter drink made from herbs. In Italy it's a small glass after dinner, for the stomach. In Argentina it's the drink of every party, mixed with cola and lots of ice: **fernet con coca**.
Argentina drinks about three quarters of all the [fernet] in the world. The only factory of the famous Italian brand outside Italy is here.

pages.prompt: At a party with no tall glasses, what do friends often mix the [fernet] in?
options: A big plastic bottle cut in half
pages.explain: The bottom half of a cola bottle becomes one huge glass, and it goes from hand to hand, like a mate.

pages.text: The home of [fernet] is **Córdoba**. People there drink more of it than anywhere else, and they will tell you so.
How much [fernet], how much cola, how much foam on top: everyone has their own rule, and everyone says the others do it wrong.

pages.prompt: The **hora del vermut** is an old custom: a drink and something small to eat. When is it?
pages.explain: **Vermut** is a wine with herbs, sweet and a little bitter, served with soda and ice. With it come olives, cheese and salami. Grandfathers did it; now young bars do too.

pages.text: The fizzy water comes from a **sifón**: a thick bottle that shoots soda when you press a handle. For a century it has been on every table next to the wine.
In many barrios the **sodero** still comes by truck once a week. He leaves full sifones and takes the empty ones. Families keep the same [sodero] for decades.

sections.title: Dichos y refranes
sections.summary: Expressions, comparisons and proverbs for exams, bores and bad luck

classes.title: Everyday expressions
classes.summary: The phrases you'll hear before lunch on any given day

pages.text: Exam tomorrow, nothing studied? **Estoy al horno**: I'm in the oven. Completely doomed? **Al horno con papas**: in the oven, with potatoes, like a Sunday roast.

pages.prompt: When you finally get something, you say **“me cayó la ficha”**: the ficha dropped. What was the ficha?
options: A token for old pay phones
A tile in a game of dominoes
A chip at the casino table
pages.explain: Old public phones ran on tokens: **fichas**, also called **cospeles**. The token dropped when the other person picked up, and then you could talk. Now it means the moment you finally understand. (A ficha is also a domino tile or a casino chip, but not here.)

pages.text: Your roommate hasn't left the couch all week, and exams start Monday. Time to tell him: **“Ponete las pilas.”** Put your batteries in. Get going.
A cancelled plan, rain on a Saturday, a two-hour line at the bank. You sigh: **“¡Qué garrón!”** What a pain.

pages.prompt: You didn't study, so in the exam you write a full page of confident nonsense. What do Argentines say you did?
options: **Pateaste el tablero**: you kicked the board
**Tiraste la toalla**: you threw in the towel
pages.explain: **Mandar fruta** is talking nonsense as if you knew. Students do it in exams, and plenty of politicians do it on TV. **Patear el tablero** is to break the rules of the game and start over. **Tirar la toalla** is to give up.

pages.text: Your friend has to go to a boring wedding alone, so you go with her. You **le hacés la gamba**: you back her up, often by going along (**gamba** is slang for leg). Ask for it: **“¿Me hacés la gamba?”**
The best thing you can say about someone is simple: **es re buena onda**. Easygoing, warm, good vibes. The coworker who never says hi? **Mala onda**. And **¡qué buena onda!** is “how nice!”

classes.title: Más contento que perro con dos colas
classes.summary: The comparisons Argentines use to exaggerate everything

pages.text: Why say “very happy” when you can be **más contento que perro con dos colas**? Happier than a dog with two tails. Argentines love a good **más … que**.
The line at the bank, a meeting, the wait for payday. Anything endless is **más largo que esperanza de pobre**: longer than a poor man's hope.

pages.prompt: A guy at the party has explained his crypto plan to you three times. Your friend whispers: **“Es más pesado que collar de…”** Heavier than a necklace of what?
pages.explain: **Más pesado que collar de melones.** **Pesado** is heavy, and also a pain. Picture wearing melons around your neck all night.

pages.text: Fake stuff is **trucho**. And nothing's faker than a bill that doesn't exist: **más trucho que billete de tres pesos**. That street-stall “original” Messi shirt? Exactly that.

The friend who can't just pick a restaurant **tiene más vueltas que una calesita**: more turns than a merry-go-round. **Dar vueltas** is to go in circles and not decide. **“No des más vueltas”**: just decide.

pages.prompt: Your friend's ex walks into the bar like he owns it. You whisper: **“Se cree la última … del desierto.”** He thinks he's the last what in the desert?
pages.explain: **La última Coca-Cola del desierto**: the one thing everybody wants. Or so he thinks. You'll hear it all over Latin America.

pages.text: And a class that won't end, or a film where nothing happens? **Más aburrido que chupar un clavo**: more boring than sucking a nail.

classes.title: Grandma's refranes
classes.summary: The old sayings every abuela has ready for any occasion

pages.text: A **refrán** is an old proverb, and most came from Spain. What's Argentine is the timing: your [abuela] has one ready before you finish telling her the problem.

And she only says half. You complain about the ugly sweater your aunt gave you: **“Y bueno, a caballo regalado…”** Everyone knows the rest: **no se le miran los dientes**. Don't look a gift horse in the mouth.

pages.prompt: After a bad breakup, your friend won't even go on a date. [Abuela] nods: **“El que se quema con leche, ve una vaca y…”** Burned by milk, you see a cow and…?
pages.explain: You cry at the sight of a cow. Once hurt, you fear anything that reminds you of it.

pages.text: New friends look a bit shady? [Abuela] raises an eyebrow: **“Decime con quién andás y te diré quién sos.”** Tell me who you hang out with, and I'll tell you who you are.
Your friend swears, again, that he starts the gym on Monday. **Del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho**: from saying to doing, it's a long way.

pages.prompt: In English, a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush. In Spanish, it's worth how many flying?
pages.explain: **Más vale pájaro en mano que cien volando.** Same lesson, much bigger flock.

pages.text: And when something goes wrong, the hopeful one: **no hay mal que por bien no venga**. There's no bad thing that doesn't bring something good.

classes.title: Argentine philosophy in seven sayings
classes.summary: The maxims that explain how the country sees itself

pages.text: Prices went up again, the train is late, the wifi is down. An Argentine shrugs: **es lo que hay**. It is what it is. You'll hear it every day.
The bank ignores your complaint? Call every day and make noise. **El que no llora no mama**: the baby who doesn't cry doesn't get fed. It's also a line in the famous tango **Cambalache**.

pages.prompt: A new tax is announced. By dinnertime, your friends already know three ways around it. They shrug: **“Hecha la ley, hecha la…”** Once the law is made, so is the what?
pages.explain: As soon as a law is made, someone finds the way around it. Said with a shrug about bureaucracy, taxes and life.

pages.text: Skipping the line, a clever shortcut, finding the loophole: that's **viveza criolla**, and the one who does it is a **vivo**. Argentines joke about it, but many hate it and blame it for the country's problems.

pages.prompt: A man cuts in front of you at the bakery. You tell him: **“No te hagas el vivo.”** What does it mean?
options: Don't try to be clever with me
Don't be in such a hurry
Don't act like you live here
pages.explain: A **vivo** gets ahead by being sly. People here take lines seriously: cut one and you will hear this.

pages.text: A fridge door held shut with a belt, a car that somehow still runs: **atado con alambre**, held together with wire. **“Lo atamos con alambre”**: we'll fix it with what we have. People are proud of that skill too.
A goal in the 94th minute, a flight you caught by seconds. When luck saves the day, someone will say it: **Dios es argentino**. God is Argentine.
And for a friend going through hard times, the kindest one: **siempre que llovió, paró**. Every time it rained, it stopped.

sections.title: Puteadas
sections.summary: Argentine swearing: what it means, and when to keep your mouth shut

classes.title: Boludo, the word that does everything
classes.summary: Greeting, insult, punctuation: one word, many jobs

pages.text: A **puteada** is a swear word or an insult. Argentines swear a lot, and often with love. The goal here: understand them, and know when to keep quiet.

pages.prompt: First week at a new job. A coworker your age says: **“Che, boludo, ¿venís a almorzar?”** What does it tell you?
options: He thinks you messed something up
He's already treating you as a friend
He's testing whether you'll push back
pages.explain: Between people who get along, **boludo** is closer to “dude” than to “idiot”. It started as an insult and got softer between friends.

pages.text: **Boludo** literally means big-balled: an idiot. But between friends it softened into “dude”. **¿Qué hacés, boludo?** is just “What's up, man?” To a woman it's **boluda**, and women say it to each other just as much.
Some [porteños] use it like a comma: **“Fui al súper, boludo, y no había nada, boludo.”**
Same word, said slowly with a stare, is still an insult. From a local friend it's warm. From a stranger with an accent, it can land like a slap.

pages.prompt: [Boludo] has a longer cousin: **pelotudo**. Compared with [boludo], how does it land?
pages.explain: **Boludo** can be love. **Pelotudo** rarely is. **¡Qué pelotudo!** means “What an idiot!”, and people mean it.

pages.text: Two milder relatives you'll hear all day: **una boludez** is something silly or very easy, as in **es una boludez**. **Boludear** is to waste time or fool around.
Say [boludo] only once your friends say it to you. Never to a waiter, a driver or someone you just met.

classes.title: Gil, forro, chanta: the cast of characters
classes.summary: The people Argentines love to complain about

pages.text: Argentines love complaining about certain kinds of people, and each kind has a name. Meet the cast.

pages.prompt: A street seller charges you triple because you're a tourist, and you pay. What does your Argentine friend call you, lovingly?
pages.explain: You got fooled, so you're the **gil**: the sucker. **No seas gil** means don't be a sucker.

pages.text: It's old [lunfardo], all over tango lyrics: the [gil] got scammed, the **vivo** did the scamming. Rude, but mild enough to tease friends with.
The **chanta** is all talk: brags, promises, never delivers. The plumber who says **“mañana paso”** for three weeks? [Chanta].
Three more you'll hear today. The **garca** cheats people or treats them badly. The **ortiva** spoils the fun, or tells on you. The **careta** is fake: acts very proper and hides what they really do.

pages.prompt: Back to the first three. Which one hurts most when said to someone's face?
pages.explain: **Forro**, by far: it attacks a person's character. **Gil** and **chanta** are closer to teasing.

pages.text: **Forro** means lining, and it's slang for condom. Said to a person, it means a nasty, selfish person: a jerk. It's about character, not brains. Understand it, never say it.
The friend who won't stop bugging you is an **hinchapelotas** (or **rompebolas**): a ball-breaker. Between friends it's a jokey complaint, not a war.
With a stranger, none of these. When in doubt, laugh and keep quiet: no [puteada] is better than the wrong one.

classes.title: La puta madre: pure frustration
classes.summary: The exclamations for when everything goes wrong

pages.text: Stub your toe, miss the bus, see the price of a coffee: **¡La puta madre!** Nobody's mother is involved. It's just “damn it!”, aimed at the universe.
It comes in levels: **la puta que lo parió**, then the maximum, **la re puta que lo parió**. Or just a long, tired **“la puta…”**

pages.prompt: You tell your friend you met Messi at the airport. She laughs: **“¡Andá a cagar!”**, literally “go take a shit”. What does she mean?
pages.explain: Laughing plus big news means disbelief. Said cold, with a door closing, the same words mean “get lost”. More usual for disbelief: **¡No jodas!** or **¡Me estás jodiendo!**, “you're kidding me!” **Joder** here is to joke or to bother.

pages.text: **Cagar**, to shit, is everywhere. **Cagarse de risa** is to laugh very hard. **Una cagada** is a mistake or something bad. **Me cagó** means “he cheated me”. Vulgar, but everyday among friends.

**La concha de tu madre** is the heavy one, very vulgar. Aimed at a person, it's a serious insult. For plain frustration, when your phone hits the floor, people shout **la concha de la lora** at nobody.
**Me chupa un huevo** (egg = testicle) means “I couldn't care less”. Very vulgar, for friends only. The clean version is **me da igual**.

pages.prompt: **Pedo** means fart. Your friend says: **“Ni en pedo voy a esa fiesta.”** Is he going to the party?
options: Yes, but only if he's drunk
pages.explain: **Ni en pedo** is “no way”. Literally: not even drunk.

pages.text: The rest of the family: **en pedo** is drunk. **Al pedo** is pointless, for nothing. **De pedo** is by pure luck. Vulgar, but very common among friends.
Need a clean version? Say **¡miércoles!** (Wednesday) for mierda and **¡la pucha!** for [la puta]. Safe with kids, bosses and grandmas.

classes.title: Reading the room
classes.summary: The stadium, the traffic, and your partner's grandma

pages.text: At **la cancha**, swearing is a sport. The referee hears **“¡Cobrá, referí!”** plus a few insults about his mother. Some fans joke it's part of the ticket price.

Chants also carry real slurs. Never repeat these: **puto**, **trolo** (against gay men), **mogólico** (mocks disability), **negro de mierda** (racist), **bolita**, **paragua** (against Bolivians, Paraguayans). But **negro**, **gordo** and **flaco** alone are loving nicknames between family and friends.

pages.prompt: In Qatar, quiet, polite Messi got angry at a Dutch player during a live TV interview: **“¿Qué mirás, bobo?”** What happened next?
options: It ended up on T-shirts and mugs
FIFA banned him for a match
pages.explain: He said “What are you looking at, fool?” **Bobo** is mild, almost childish, which made it even funnier. Within days it was a national catchphrase.

pages.text: **Hijo de puta** is a heavy insult. But after a great goal or a very good joke, **¡qué hijo de puta!** is admiration: “what a genius!” The tone and the smile decide. Understand it, and leave it to the locals.
Buenos Aires traffic makes even calm people swear. Green light, one second: **¡Dale, boludo!** Cut off: **¿Quién te dio el registro?**, who gave you a license? Usually it's just venting.
Before you swear, ask: would I say this in front of my partner's grandma? If not, save it for close friends. With your boss, a cop or a stranger, keep it clean.

pages.prompt: In 2009, right after qualifying for the World Cup, coach Maradona told journalists on live TV: **“que la chupen”**, suck it. What happened?
options: FIFA banned him for two months
He was fired the next week
pages.explain: FIFA banned him for two months and fined him. He was talking to the journalists who had doubted him. Argentines, meanwhile, turned the line into a classic.

pages.text: Start safe: **¡la pucha!**, **¡qué bajón!** (that's too bad), **¡uh, no!** Add **boludo** later, once your friends say it to you.

sections.title: Música
sections.summary: Rock nacional, folklore, cumbia, trap, and crowds louder than the band

classes.title: Rock nacional
classes.summary: Rock in Spanish, born in a café bathroom and raised under a dictatorship

pages.text: Before 1967, rock here meant copies: foreign hits, translated or sung in English. Then **Los Gatos** released **“La balsa”**, an original song in Spanish, and it sold. **Rock nacional** was born.

pages.prompt: The story goes that “La balsa” was started somewhere unusual. Where?
options: In the bathroom of an all-night café
In a police cell, after a noisy night out
On a ferry crossing the Río de la Plata
pages.explain: **Tanguito** came up with the opening in the bathroom of **La Perla del Once**, an all-night café where young musicians met. **Litto Nebbia** finished the song. At least, that's the legend.

pages.text: Two names you must know. **Luis Alberto Spinetta**, **el Flaco**, wrote dreamy, poetic songs like **“Muchacha (ojos de papel)”**. **Charly García** became the wild genius: brilliant, unpredictable, loved. Start with **“Los dinosaurios”**.

pages.prompt: Charly once made a famous exit from a ninth-floor hotel room in Mendoza. How?
options: He jumped out the window into the pool
He climbed down on knotted bedsheets
He slid down the laundry chute
pages.explain: Ninth floor, into the pool, and he walked away. It's rock legend now, though it came from a rough time in his life.

pages.text: Under the 1976–83 dictatorship, rock was censored and harassed, so musicians sang in metaphors. For many kids, a concert was the only place they could feel free together.

pages.prompt: Then came the 1982 [Malvinas] war against Britain. What happened to Argentine rock on the radio?
options: It took over, because English songs were pulled
It was banned completely until the war ended
pages.explain: The regime that harassed rockers suddenly needed Spanish songs to fill the airwaves. Bands went from underground to mainstream almost overnight.

pages.text: **Soda Stereo** took Argentine rock across Latin America. At their farewell show in 1997, **Gustavo Cerati** closed with **“¡Gracias… totales!”** People still say it, half joking, for a very big thank you.
More names you'll hear at every party: **Fito Páez**, **Andrés Calamaro**, **Los Fabulosos Cadillacs** and **Divididos**. Everyone in the room knows the words.

classes.title: Folklore, peñas and pañuelos
classes.summary: Guitars, handkerchiefs and the voice of La Negra

pages.text: In Argentina **folklore** isn't museum music. It's the living sound of the provinces: guitars, violins and the **bombo legüero**, a deep drum of wood and hide.
Its rhythms have names. **Zamba** and **chacarera** come from the northwest. **Chamamé**, played with accordion, comes from the northeast. Young people still sing them at parties.
**Mercedes Sosa**, from Tucumán, was **La Negra**, a nickname said with love. Her version of **“Gracias a la vida”**, by Chile's Violeta Parra, still makes whole rooms cry.

pages.prompt: During the dictatorship, where was Mercedes Sosa arrested?
options: On stage, in the middle of a concert
At the airport, back from a tour
At home, while writing a song
pages.explain: She was arrested mid-concert in La Plata in 1979, along with the audience, and went into exile in Europe. She came back in 1982, still under the dictatorship, and packed theater after theater.

pages.text: A **peña** is a folklore night: long tables, **empanadas**, wine and live music. Nobody just sits and watches. When a [chacarera] starts, people dance between the tables, then sit down and keep eating.

pages.prompt: The **zamba** is a slow dance for couples, with a white handkerchief. How do they use it?
options: They wave it while circling, never touching
They tie it around their partner's wrist
They drop it for the other to pick up
pages.explain: The **pañuelo**, the handkerchief, turns the zamba into slow flirting. And no, it's not the Brazilian samba. The fast one, with stomping and finger snaps, is the **chacarera**.

pages.text: Every January, the small town of **Cosquín**, in the Córdoba hills, hosts the national folk festival: nine nights, **las nueve lunas**. Each night opens with a shout: **“¡Aquí Cosquín!”**
Invited to dance at a [peña]? Say **“¡Dale!”** and get up. Nobody expects a foreigner to dance well. Getting up is what counts.

classes.title: Cumbia and cuarteto
classes.summary: The bailanta, a cumbia saint, and the tunga tunga from Córdoba

pages.text: Rock fills stadiums, but **cumbia** fills the dance floor. Born in Colombia, it became deeply Argentine in the dance halls of the suburbs: the **bailantas**.
At every wedding the DJ eventually puts on [cumbia], and even your serious uncle turns out to be a **cumbiero**. You don't have to like it. You just have to dance.

pages.prompt: **Gilda** became one of the biggest [cumbia] stars of the 90s. What was her job before?
pages.explain: She was a **maestra jardinera**, a kindergarten teacher, and only became a star in her 30s, in a scene run by men. Her **“No me arrepiento de este amor”** is still sung everywhere.

pages.text: In 1996 Gilda died when a truck hit her tour bus on **Ruta 12**, in Entre Ríos. People began asking her for miracles at a shrine by the road. The Church never made her a saint. The people did.
In the late 90s, with the economy collapsing, a rawer style grew in the poorest neighborhoods: **cumbia villera**. Critics hear crude lyrics. Fans hear the honest voice of the barrio.
In **Córdoba** the party sound is **cuarteto**, with a bouncy piano beat everyone calls **tunga tunga**. Its king, **La Mona Jiménez**, has played packed dances for decades.

pages.prompt: In 2025 [cuarteto] got an honor that tango got back in 2009. Which one?
options: A place on UNESCO's heritage list
A national day off in its name
pages.explain: UNESCO added cuarteto to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage. Not bad for music born in Córdoba's dance halls.

pages.text: **Rodrigo**, **el Potro**, took [cuarteto] to Buenos Aires and filled the Luna Park. He died young, in a car crash after a show. **“Soy cordobés”** and **“La mano de Dios”**, his song for Maradona, still close every party.
And today? You'll hear **Los Palmeras**, from Santa Fe, with **“Bombón asesino”**, the [cumbia] of **Ke Personajes**, and the [cuarteto] of **La K'onga**.

classes.title: Trap, RKT and Bizarrap
classes.summary: From freestyle battles in a park to the biggest stages in the world

pages.text: Argentine trap and rap fill stadiums now. Its big names, like **Duki**, **Trueno** and **Wos**, didn't come from music schools or record labels.

pages.prompt: So where did they learn?
options: Rap battles on the steps of a park
Singing in church choirs as kids
Busking for coins on the subte
pages.explain: For years, kids met on the steps of **Parque Rivadavia** for **El Quinto Escalón**: free freestyle battles, and the crowd shouted for the winner.

pages.text: **Bizarrap** is a producer who hides behind a cap and dark glasses. In his **BZRP Music Sessions**, one guest raps or sings over his beat in a tiny studio.

pages.prompt: Before producing, how did Bizarrap get known on YouTube?
pages.explain: He cut and posted clips of battles like the Quinto Escalón. The scene that made Duki and Trueno made him too.

pages.text: A session with **el Biza**, as everyone calls him, can launch a career overnight. In 2023 his session with **Shakira**, a song aimed at her ex, broke YouTube records.
Women run the charts too: **María Becerra** sold out River's stadium, **Tini** went from Disney star to pop queen, and **Nicki Nicole** broke out of Rosario.

pages.prompt: One big party sound of the 2020s is **RKT**. Where does the name come from?
pages.explain: DJs at **Rescate**, a club in San Martín, just outside the city, started mixing it. “RKT” is a short form of the club's name, and the sound kept it.

pages.text: RKT is reggaetón plus [cumbia villera], with huge bass. **L-Gante** made it explode, recording his first hits on a laptop the government gave out to schoolkids. He calls his style **cumbia 420**.

classes.title: Live: pogo, bengalas and misas
classes.summary: Why foreign bands leave Argentina a little shaken

pages.text: At a **recital** here, the crowd doesn't just listen. It sings every word, often louder than the band. Foreign artists leave a little shaken.

pages.prompt: The Rolling Stones named a whole documentary after something Latin American crowds do. What?
options: The way fans camp out for days
The flares they light in the stands
pages.explain: *Olé, Olé, Olé!* Between songs, the stadium sings it football style, followed by the artist's name: **“Olé, olé, olé, olé… Charly, Charly!”**

pages.text: Argentina has so many Stones fans they have a name: **rollingas**. When a band walks off before the encore, the stadium shouts **“¡Otra, otra!”**, or sings **“una más, y no jodemos más”**: one more and we'll stop bothering you.
**Los Redondos**, led by singer **el Indio Solari**, barely talked to the press, yet fans crossed the country to see them. Fans didn't call the shows concerts. They called them **misas**: masses.

pages.prompt: Near the stage, hundreds of people jump and crash into each other: the **pogo**. What happens if someone falls?
options: The people closest pick them up
pages.explain: It looks like chaos, but it has a code: **si alguien se cae, se lo levanta**. Whoever falls gets picked up.

pages.text: In the 90s, barrio rock crowds, **rock chabón**, brought the football stadium to gigs: banners, chants and **bengalas**, flares lit right in the crowd.

The flares had a dark side. On December 30, 2004, at a **Callejeros** show at **República Cromañón**, a flare set the ceiling on fire. The club was overcrowded, an exit was locked. **194 people died**, most of them young.
It changed live music forever: much stricter rules, and a flare indoors is now unthinkable. Every December 30, families still gather to remember.

sections.title: Tango
sections.summary: The music of the Río de la Plata: where it came from, what it sings about, and how to behave at a milonga

classes.title: Born on the edge of town
classes.summary: Two cities, one port, and a German squeezebox

pages.text: Tango was born in the late 1800s in the **arrabal**, the rough edge of town: **conventillos** (crowded shared houses), corner bars, the port. The music of immigrants, sailors, workers and Afro-Argentines, with African rhythms like **candombe** in the mix.

pages.prompt: Polite Buenos Aires society found tango scandalous. What finally changed their minds?
options: A president danced it in public
It became a craze in Paris
The Church gave it its blessing
pages.explain: Once Paris loved it, the rich loved it too. Nothing like European approval to change the mind of a porteño, a Buenos Aires local.

pages.text: Around 1900, men far outnumbered women in the city. So men often practiced tango with each other until they were good enough to dance with a woman.

pages.prompt: The most famous tango ever, **La Cumparsita**, was written where?
pages.explain: Gerardo Matos Rodríguez, a young Uruguayan student, wrote it around 1916, and it premiered in a Montevideo café. Milongas, tango dance nights, still play it as the last tango of the night.

pages.text: So tango isn't only Argentine. It's **rioplatense**, from both sides of the river. In 2009 UNESCO listed it as heritage of both countries, and Uruguayans will remind you.
The sound of tango is the **bandoneón**, and it's German. The story goes it was meant for small churches with no organ. It crossed the ocean with immigrants, and went from hymns to tango bars.

pages.prompt: Why is the [bandoneón] famously hard to play?
options: Each button plays two different notes
It's as heavy as a small piano
It only plays in a single key
pages.explain: The note changes depending on whether the bellows open or close. Tango musicians call it **el fueye**: the bellows.

pages.text: Early tango was quick and playful, played on flute, violin and guitar. Many say the [bandoneón] slowed it down, and that's where tango got its famous sadness.

classes.title: At the milonga
classes.summary: The unwritten rules of the dance floor

pages.text: A **milonga** is a tango dance night: tables around a wooden floor, a DJ or a live orquesta, every age dancing until late. Buenos Aires has one every night of the week.

pages.prompt: At a traditional [milonga], how do you ask someone to dance?
options: Walk to their table and offer your hand
Catch their eye across the room and nod
Ask the DJ to dedicate them a song
pages.explain: That's the **cabeceo**: a look, a small nod. If they nod back, you go get them.

pages.text: And if they look away? That's a no, and nobody got rejected in public. That's the whole point of the [cabeceo].

Music comes in **tandas**, sets of 3 or 4 songs: tango, **vals**, or **milonga**, which is also the name of a faster, happier rhythm. Then a short non-tango **cortina** plays, and everyone changes partners.

pages.prompt: Your partner says **“gracias”** after the first song. What just happened?
pages.explain: Just like with mate, **gracias** mid-tanda means “thanks, that's enough”. Want to keep going? Chat a little between songs and save **gracias** for the end of the tanda.

pages.text: Couples hold each other in the **abrazo**, the embrace, and move counterclockwise in a **ronda**, like cars on a track. No overtaking, no high kicks, and never teach your partner on the floor.
The dinner shows with flying legs and a rose in someone's mouth? [Porteños] call that **tango for export**. At a [milonga], the dance is small, close and improvised.
One honest note: most Argentines don't dance tango. It's a small, devoted scene, with many foreigners in it. But almost everyone knows the songs.

classes.title: Gardel
classes.summary: The voice, the smile, and the question of where he was born

pages.text: **Carlos Gardel** is *the* tango singer, and Argentina's first pop idol. Slicked-back hair, a movie-star smile, a voice people still call perfect.

pages.prompt: Where do most researchers say Gardel was born?
pages.explain: Most researchers say **Toulouse**. But Gardel once signed papers saying **Tacuarembó**, Uruguay, and many Uruguayans still claim him.

pages.text: Argentines settle it simply: he grew up in **Abasto**, the market barrio, so he's porteño. They call him **el Morocho del Abasto**.
In 1935, at the peak of his fame, Gardel died in a plane crash in **Medellín**, Colombia, while on tour. The whole country went into mourning.

pages.prompt: At his tomb in Chacarita cemetery, what do fans leave in his bronze statue's hand?
options: A folded page of sheet music
pages.explain: A lit **pucho**, slang for cigarette. Legend says if it burns all the way down, your wish comes true.

pages.text: His fans' favorite line: **cada día canta mejor**, he sings better every day. Almost a century later, and still improving.
His name is also a compliment. **Sos Gardel** means you're the best, or you have all you need: **“Con un asado y amigos, sos Gardel.”**
Someone keeps complaining about something you can't fix? **Andá a cantarle a Gardel**: go sing it to Gardel, nobody here will listen. It's dismissive, so keep it for friends.

classes.title: Big bands and a rebel
classes.summary: When tango was pop music, and the man who was told “eso no es tango”

pages.text: In the **1940s**, tango was pop music. Every club and radio station had an **orquesta típica**, and people followed bandleaders like football teams.
Tango DJs still build whole nights around them: **D'Arienzo**, punchy and rhythmic. **Di Sarli**, smooth and elegant. **Pugliese**, dark and dramatic.

pages.prompt: Pugliese was a communist and was jailed more than once. What did his orquesta do while he was inside?
options: Cancelled every show until he was freed
Played on, with a red carnation on his piano
Hired a new pianist and never looked back
pages.explain: A **clavel rojo**, a red carnation, on the empty piano. Everyone in the room got the message. Musicians still say **“¡Pugliese, Pugliese, Pugliese!”** for good luck before a show.

pages.text: Then came the rebel: **Astor Piazzolla**. He grew up in New York, where his dad gave him a [bandoneón] as a kid.

pages.prompt: At 13, Piazzolla had a tiny part as a newspaper boy in a Gardel film shot in New York, and Gardel invited him on his 1935 tour. What happened?
options: His father said he was too young
He joined and played every show
He said no to keep studying piano
pages.explain: His father saved his life. That was Gardel's last tour: it ended in the plane crash in Medellín.

pages.text: Back in Buenos Aires he played [bandoneón] in the orquesta of **Aníbal Troilo**, the most loved bandleader of all, then studied classical music in Paris with **Nadia Boulanger**. She told him to stop hiding his tango.

So he mixed tango with jazz and classical: **nuevo tango**. Think **Libertango** and **Adiós Nonino**. Traditionalists called him **el asesino del tango**, and **“eso no es tango”** followed him for years.
Today he's among the most played Argentine composers in the world, and tango keeps changing: bands like **Bajofondo** and **Gotan Project** mix it with electronic beats.

classes.title: What tango sings about
classes.summary: Mom, the barrio, the woman who left, and a world gone wrong

pages.text: Tango lyrics have favorite subjects: the woman who left (always her fault), mom (a saint), the old barrio, and nostalgia for everything.
Tango poet **Discépolo** summed it up: **el tango es un pensamiento triste que se baila**. A sad thought you can dance to.

pages.prompt: Gardel's **Volver** has tango's most quoted line. What does it claim?
pages.explain: **“Que veinte años no es nada.”** Twenty years is nothing. The words are by **Alfredo Le Pera**, Gardel's writing partner. Heard at reunions and birthdays, anywhere time has passed and everyone pretends it hasn't.

pages.text: **Mi Buenos Aires querido** is a man far away, dreaming of coming home. Ask any Argentine living abroad whether it makes them cry.

**Cambalache**, also by Discépolo, isn't about love. Written in 1934, it says the world is a junk shop where **“lo mismo un burro que un gran profesor”**: a donkey and a great professor count the same.

pages.prompt: What happened to **Cambalache** in the 1940s?
options: It was banned from the radio
It won a national music prize
pages.explain: In 1943 the military government banned slang from the radio, to “protect” the language, and Cambalache went with it. Being banned only made it more famous. It still sounds like this morning's news.

pages.text: That slang is **lunfardo**, and tango carried it everywhere. Words from its lyrics like **mina** (woman), **laburo** (work) and **guita** (money) are still used every day.
Its name stuck, too. When something is a total, unfair mess, Argentines sigh: **“esto es un cambalache.”**

sections.title: Games
sections.summary: A card game for liars, football stickers and dream numbers

classes.title: Truco
classes.summary: The national card game, and how partners talk without words

pages.text: **Truco** is the national card game. People play it in bars, on the beach, at school breaks and after every [asado], usually two against two.

pages.prompt: What is the most important skill in [truco]?
pages.explain: You shout **“¡Truco!”** to raise the bet, even with terrible cards. The other team must decide if you're lying. **Mentir**, to lie, is part of the rules.

pages.text: It's played with Spanish cards, not hearts and clubs. The four suits are **espadas** (swords), **bastos** (wooden clubs), **oros** (gold coins) and **copas** (cups).
The strongest card is the 1 of swords: the **ancho de espada**. Nothing beats it.

pages.prompt: In the middle of a game, your partner looks at you and lifts both eyebrows. What does it mean?
pages.explain: Partners talk with secret faces, the **señas**. Lifted eyebrows: the ancho de espada. A wink: the second best card. The trick is that the other team must not see.

pages.text: A game goes to 30 points. The first fifteen are the **malas**, the bad ones, and the last fifteen are the **buenas**. Points are counted with matches or dry beans.
[Truco] gave words to everyday talk. **Retrucar** is to answer back fast in an argument. **Irse al mazo**, to go to the pile, is to give up.

classes.title: Figuritas
classes.summary: The sticker album that drives the whole country crazy

pages.text: **Figuritas** are small stickers of football players that you collect in an album. Every World Cup, children and adults go a little crazy to fill theirs.

pages.prompt: In 2022 there were not enough [figuritas] in the kioscos. What did the government do?
options: It called a meeting about it
It set a limit of one pack per child
pages.explain: A real government meeting about football stickers, with the company that makes them and the kiosco owners. Three months later Argentina won the World Cup.

pages.text: Nobody fills an album alone. You swap. A friend shows you a pile, one by one, and you answer fast: **“late”** (I have it) or **“nola”** (I don't).
Those two words are **la tengo** and **no la tengo**, cut short. The sticker that almost nobody has is **la difícil**, the hard one.

pages.prompt: At school, children also play to win each other's [figuritas]. How?
options: They hide them and the others look for them
They throw them at a wall, and the closest one wins
They race to stick them in the album
pages.explain: That game is **el espejito**. In another one, **la tapadita**, your figurita has to land on top of someone else's. The winner takes both.

pages.text: Adults do it too. In a World Cup year, offices have a list on the wall of who needs which number, and nobody finds that strange.
On weekends, in some parks, people of all ages meet to swap [figuritas]. Parents say it's for the children. It's not always true.

classes.title: Dream numbers
classes.summary: The small daily lottery and its list of numbers

pages.text: **La quiniela** is a lottery with several draws a day. The simple bet is a number from 00 to 99: you bet a little money at an **agencia**, a small lottery shop.

pages.prompt: How do many players choose their number?
options: From what they dreamed last night
From the price of the dollar
From the result of the last football game
pages.explain: Every number has a meaning, and every dream has a number. The list hangs on the wall of every agencia.

pages.text: Some of the list: **00** is eggs, **14** is the drunk man, **15** is the pretty girl, **17** is bad luck, **32** is money.

pages.prompt: One number is called **los dos patitos**, the two little ducks, because of how it looks. Which one?
pages.explain: Two 2s look like two ducks swimming. In the dream list, 22 is also **el loco**, the crazy man.

pages.text: The most famous is **48**: **il morto che parla**, “the dead man who talks”. The name is Italian, because the list came with the immigrants from Naples.
People also play the number plate of a car that crashed, or the age of a famous person who just died. When something big happens, half the country bets on the same number.
Tell a neighbor you dreamed of your dead grandfather talking, and you'll hear **“jugale al 48”**: bet on 48. It's a joke and real advice at once.

sections.title: Summer and holidays
sections.summary: An empty city, a cold sea, carnival and weekend trips

classes.title: January: everybody out
classes.summary: The city goes quiet and the road to the sea fills up

pages.text: In January, Buenos Aires is half empty. No traffic, free seats on the [subte], and paper signs on shop doors: **“Cerrado por vacaciones.”**

pages.prompt: Where did all those [porteños] go?
options: To the mountains in the west
To the beaches of the Atlantic
To their families in Italy and Spain
pages.explain: They call it **la Costa**: a long line of beach towns about 400 km away, in the province of Buenos Aires. The biggest is **Mar del Plata**.

pages.text: There's a verb for it: **veranear**, to spend the summer somewhere. Many families go back to the same town, and the same street, for decades.
Holidays are counted in halves of a month. A **quincena** is fifteen days: **“Nos vamos la primera quincena de enero.”**

pages.prompt: What is the sea like on the Costa?
options: Warm and flat, like a lake
Clear and blue, with white sand
pages.explain: Few people go for the water. They go for the family, the friends, the nights and the same beach as every year.

pages.text: Each town has its own crowd. **Pinamar** and **Cariló** are expensive. **Villa Gesell** is for the young. **Mar del Plata** is for everyone, and its nickname is **La Feliz**: the happy one.
The day one [quincena] ends and the next begins is famous for its traffic. The TV news shows the road to the Costa live, hour by hour.

classes.title: A day at the beach
classes.summary: The kit, the sellers, the games and the nights

pages.text: The beach kit: a **reposera** (a folding chair), a **sombrilla** (a big umbrella), a **heladerita** (a small box that keeps drinks cold), and of course the [termo] and the [mate].
A **balneario** is a beach club. There, families rent a **carpa**, a small cloth tent, for the whole summer. Some have had the same [carpa] for three generations.

pages.prompt: Sellers walk on the sand all day, shouting. What is the classic thing they sell?
pages.explain: **“¡Churros, hay churros!”** Filled with dulce de leche and eaten with sandy fingers. Also **choclo**, corn, and ice cream.

pages.text: Beach games: **tejo**, where you throw flat discs as close as you can to a small one, and **paleta**, two wooden bats and a ball.

pages.prompt: Suddenly the whole beach starts to clap in rhythm. What is happening?
pages.explain: An adult lifts the lost child onto their shoulders and walks. Everyone claps so the parents look, and the clapping follows the child along the beach.

pages.text: At night nobody stays in. Families walk on the **peatonal**, the street without cars, eat more churros and play old video games, the **fichines**.
In summer, the stars of TV move to Mar del Plata too, and act in a theater there every night. Seeing a show is part of the holiday.

classes.title: Carnival, three ways
classes.summary: Feathers by the river, drums in the barrio and the mountains of Jujuy

pages.text: **Carnaval** comes in February or March, with two public holidays. Argentina has three very different ones.

pages.prompt: Which place has the biggest carnival in the country, with feathers and huge moving stages?
options: Gualeguaychú, a small city by a river
pages.explain: In **Gualeguaychú**, in Entre Ríos, groups compete every Saturday of January and February on a long avenue built just for it. It looks like Rio in a small size.

pages.text: In Buenos Aires, each barrio has a **murga**: neighbors of all ages in shiny suits who dance with high kicks behind big drums.
They perform at a **corso**: a street closed for the night. Children run around with cans of white foam, and nobody goes home clean.
[Murga] songs make fun of politicians and the news of the year. The last dictatorship took away the carnival holidays. They only came back in 2011.

pages.prompt: In the mountain villages of Jujuy, how does carnival begin?
options: They ring the church bells all night
They dig a small devil out of the ground
They throw water from the roofs
pages.explain: The **diablito**, the little devil, was buried at the end of last year's carnival. Out he comes, and for about a week people dance, covered in flour and paper ribbons. Then they bury him again.

pages.text: The rest of the year has parties too. Hundreds of towns hold a **Fiesta Nacional** for what they make: the apple, the salami, the wheat, the flower, the trout.

classes.title: Short trips and winter
classes.summary: Islands near the city, Brazil in Spanish and a house for the day

pages.text: A short trip of two or three days is an **escapada**. A Monday holiday makes a **finde largo**, a long weekend, and the roads fill up.
The closest one is **Tigre**, less than an hour from Buenos Aires: hundreds of green islands and brown rivers. People live there in wooden houses with no streets.

pages.prompt: How do the children of those islands get to school?
pages.explain: A school boat stops at each house, like a bus. There is also a shop boat, a doctor boat and a boat that takes the rubbish.

pages.text: A **quinta** is a house outside the city with a garden and a pool. Groups of friends rent one for a single day: [asado], pool, football, home at night.

pages.prompt: For warm sea, Argentines drive to Brazil. One Brazilian city gets so many that shops and menus are in Spanish. Which one?
pages.explain: People call it **Floripa**. In January, on some of its beaches, you hear more Argentine Spanish than Portuguese.

pages.text: In July, schools close for two weeks: the **vacaciones de invierno**. Families with money go to the snow. In the city, cinemas and children's theaters are full.
Another classic is **Colonia**, in Uruguay, one hour by boat across the river: old stone streets, a lighthouse, lunch, and back the same night.

sections.title: School and work
sections.summary: School rituals, university, how people work and how they protest

classes.title: At school
classes.summary: A white coat, half a day of class and exams in summer

pages.text: In public primary schools, children wear a white coat over their clothes: the **guardapolvo blanco**. Rich or poor, everyone looks the same. That was the idea.

pages.prompt: In which month does the school year start?
pages.explain: School runs from March to December. The long holidays are in summer, and summer here is December to March.

pages.text: Most children go to school for half a day: **turno mañana** or **turno tarde**, the morning or the afternoon group. A full day is **jornada completa**.
In primary school the teacher is **la seño**, short for *señorita*, even if she is sixty and married. In secondary school, every teacher is **profe**.
Each morning the flag goes up. The student with the best marks carries it at school events: the **abanderado** or **abanderada**. Families are very proud of it.

pages.prompt: A secondary student fails maths at the end of the year. What happens?
options: They repeat the whole year right away
They pay for extra classes at the school
They study in summer and take an exam again
pages.explain: The phrase is **llevarse una materia**: to carry a subject with you into the holidays. **“Me llevé matemática”** means a summer with books.

pages.text: Marks go from 1 to 10. You pass with a 6 or a 7, depending on the province. And skipping school for a day has its own name: **ratearse**.

classes.title: The last year of school
classes.summary: A year of rituals before school ends

pages.text: The last year of secondary school is one long party. The students who are finishing are the **egresados**, and the whole year has rituals.
Each class designs its own hoodie, the **buzo de egresados**, with a name for the group on the front and everyone's nickname on the back. They wear it all year.

pages.prompt: How do many students arrive at school on the first day of their last year?
options: In their parents' cars, all in a line
With no sleep, after a party that lasted all night
pages.explain: It's the **UPD**, the *Último Primer Día*: the last first day. They party all night and walk into school at sunrise with drums and flags.

pages.text: Then comes the **viaje de egresados**: one week away with the whole class and no parents. Families pay for it in small parts over two years.

pages.prompt: Where do most classes go for that trip?
options: To the beach in Mar del Plata
To the mountains and lakes of Bariloche
