pages.explain: **Bariloche**, in Patagonia: snow, trips by day and dancing every night. Whole planes and buses of 17-year-olds arrive all winter.

pages.text: The year ends with the **fiesta de egresados**: a formal party with parents and grandparents at dinner. After midnight the adults go home, and the dancing goes on until morning.
The day the trip ends, parents wait for the bus at dawn. The children come back with no voice, no sleep and a bag of dirty clothes.

classes.title: University is free
classes.summary: No fees, no campus and a very messy last day

pages.text: Public universities in Argentina charge nothing to study. The biggest is the **UBA**, the Universidad de Buenos Aires, with more than 300,000 students.

pages.prompt: The [UBA] has no entrance exam. What do you do instead?
options: A first year of general subjects
Nothing: you wait for a free place
pages.explain: It's the **CBC**, the *Ciclo Básico Común*. Anyone can start it. Passing all of it is the hard part.

pages.text: People don't say university. They say **la facultad**, or **la facu**: **“Estoy en la facu.”** There is no campus life. Students live at home and take the bus.
Many students work and study at the same time, so a degree can take seven or eight years. The big exam at the end of each subject is a **final**.

pages.prompt: You see a young woman in the street covered in eggs, flour and paint. She's smiling. What happened?
options: She just passed her last exam
pages.explain: The verb is **recibirse**: to finish your degree. Friends and family wait outside the last exam with eggs, flour and anything that makes a mess.

pages.text: After that, the title is used. Lawyers and doctors are called **doctor** or **doctora**. On papers you'll see **Lic.** and **Ing.** before a name.
In 1918, students in **Córdoba** took over their university and won the right to help run it. The **Reforma Universitaria** was copied all over Latin America.

classes.title: Work
classes.summary: Jobs with and without papers, and life at the office

pages.text: The everyday word for a job is **laburo**, and to work is **laburar**. **“Tengo mucho laburo”**: I have a lot of work. **“¿De qué laburás?”**: what do you do?

pages.prompt: In June and in December, registered workers get something extra. What?
options: A box of food and wine
pages.explain: It's the **aguinaldo**: one extra salary a year, paid in two halves. People plan holidays and big purchases around it.

pages.text: A job is **en blanco**, in white, when it is registered: [aguinaldo], paid holidays, health cover. **En negro**, in black, means no papers. More than a third of workers are [en negro].
People who work for themselves pay one small fixed tax every month, the **monotributo**. A client will ask: **“¿Me hacés factura?”** Can you give me an invoice?

pages.prompt: It's your birthday and you work in an office. Who brings the **facturas** (sweet pastries) for everyone?
options: The person at the next desk
pages.explain: The birthday person brings the pastries for the team. Arrive with empty hands and people will joke about it all day.

pages.text: Unions, **sindicatos**, are strong. Each year they sit down with companies to raise salaries along with prices. Those talks are the **paritarias**, and they are always in the news.
After work, colleagues go for a drink: the **after office**, said in English. Wednesday and Thursday are the big days.

classes.title: The day nothing runs
classes.summary: Paros, piquetes and pots banged on balconies

pages.text: Protest is part of normal life. A **paro** is a strike: **paro de subte**, **paro de colectivos**, **paro bancario**. Locals check the news before they leave home.

pages.prompt: The unions call a **paro general**, a strike of everyone. What does Buenos Aires look like that day?
options: Like a normal day, only slower
Like a Sunday: quiet streets, few buses
Full of traffic, because everyone drives
pages.explain: No trains, no subway, few buses, no banks, almost no flights. Many people work from home or don't work.

pages.text: A **piquete** is a group of people who block a street or a road to protest. The blocked street is a **corte**. Radio and map apps list the day's cortes every morning.
A **marcha** is a march. Most of them end at **Plaza de Mayo** or at **Congreso**, with drums, flags and smoke from the [choripán] stands.
Most marches are calm and full of families. Still, traffic stops for hours, so on those days many people leave work early or stay home.

pages.prompt: It's nine at night. On every balcony, neighbors are hitting pots with spoons. What is it?
options: A party for a football title
A call for a lost dog
pages.explain: A **cacerolazo**, from **cacerola**, cooking pot. You protest from your own window, and the noise travels from building to building.

pages.text: Two questions that save your day: **“¿Hay paro mañana?”** Is there a strike tomorrow? And **“¿Está cortado?”** Is the street blocked?

sections.title: Sports beyond fútbol
sections.summary: A game with a duck, cloned horses, Pumas and the club on the corner

classes.title: The national sport is not fútbol
classes.summary: A gaucho game on horses that started with a real duck

pages.text: By law, Argentina's national sport is not football. Since 1953 it's **pato**, a game played on horses.

pages.prompt: **Pato** means duck. Why does the game have that name?
options: The first players were duck hunters
At the start, the ball was a duck, often alive, in a bag
The riders move their arms like wings
pages.explain: Gauchos from two ranches fought for the duck and raced with it to their own house. Today it's a leather ball with six handles.

pages.text: Now two teams of four riders pass the ball and throw it through a ring high on a pole. It looks like basketball on horses.
The ball often falls. A rider must pick it up from the ground without stopping, hanging off one side of the horse at full speed.

pages.prompt: The old game was wild, and riders died. What did the Church do about it?
options: It asked players to wear a cross
It moved the games to Sundays after mass
It refused to bury players who died in a game
pages.explain: The government banned pato more than once in the 1800s too. In the 1930s it came back with rules, and nobody gets killed anymore.

pages.text: The Church's order came in 1796, and Buenos Aires banned the game in 1822. [Gauchos] kept playing anyway, far from the towns.
The truth: most Argentines have never seen a game of [pato]. Every few years someone asks Congress to make football the national sport, and nothing changes.

classes.title: The best in the world at polo
classes.summary: Ten-goal players, special horses and a field in the city

pages.text: In one sport Argentina is the best by far: **polo**. Nearly all the best players in the world are Argentine, and so are the best horses.
Each player has a number from −2 to 10, the **handicap**. Only a few people in the world are a 10, and almost all of them are from here.

pages.prompt: The star **Adolfo Cambiaso** loved one horse so much that he did something new. What?
options: He made copies of her in a lab
He built her a house next to his
He stopped playing when she got old
pages.explain: They are clones. In 2016 he won the biggest tournament in the world riding six copies of the same mare, **Cuartetera**.

pages.text: That tournament is the **Abierto de Palermo**, played every spring on a field in the middle of Buenos Aires. Anyone can buy a ticket.

pages.prompt: You're left-handed and you want to play polo. What happens?
options: You play on the left side of the field
You must play with your right hand
pages.explain: It's the rule, to avoid crashes between horses: everyone holds the stick in the right hand.

pages.text: Argentina's first Olympic gold medal ever was in polo, in Paris in 1924. The game had arrived fifty years earlier with British ranch owners.
A player changes horse many times in one game, so each one brings eight or more. The best horses fly around the world with their riders.

classes.title: Pumas, Leonas and bats
classes.summary: Why every national team has an animal name

pages.text: Argentine national teams have animal names. The rugby team is **Los Pumas**. The women's hockey team is **Las Leonas**, the lionesses.

pages.prompt: Look at the Pumas' shirt. Which animal is really on it?
pages.explain: It's a yaguareté, a jaguar. On a tour in 1965, a journalist saw it, wrote “Pumas”, and the wrong name stayed forever.

pages.text: [Las Leonas] won two World Cups and four Olympic medals in a row. Their star, **Luciana Aymar**, was chosen best player in the world eight times.

pages.prompt: One national football team is called **Los Murciélagos**, the bats. Why?
pages.explain: It's football for blind players; only the goalkeeper can see. The ball makes a sound, and the crowd must be silent. They have been world champions more than once.

pages.text: Rugby is played in clubs, mostly by people who don't get paid for it. After the game comes the **tercer tiempo**, the third half: both teams eat together.
In 2020 the Pumas beat New Zealand's All Blacks for the first time, after 35 years of trying. Players and fans cried on TV.
Other teams have animal names too: **Los Leones** (men's hockey) and **Las Panteras** (women's volleyball). The handball team chose **Los Gladiadores**.

classes.title: Fangio and the fierreros
classes.summary: Five titles, a strange trip to Cuba and Ford against Chevrolet

pages.text: **Juan Manuel Fangio** won five Formula 1 world titles in the 1950s, with four different teams. Nobody won more for almost half a century.

pages.prompt: In 1958 Fangio went to Cuba for a race and never started it. Why?
options: His car was stolen from the hotel
He was kidnapped by Fidel Castro's rebels
He missed the boat from Miami
pages.explain: They wanted the world's attention. They treated him well and let him go about a day later, after the race. He said later he had nothing against them.

pages.text: A fan of cars and engines is a **fierrero**, from **fierro**, iron. The most loved racing series is **Turismo Carretera**, run since 1937.
There, the question is not Boca or River. It's **Ford or Chevrolet**. Families pick one, and the choice goes from father to child.

pages.prompt: In 1981 the Argentine **Carlos Reutemann** lost the Formula 1 title in the last race. By how much?
pages.explain: One single point. Years later he became governor of his province, Santa Fe. Everyone called him by his nickname, **Lole**.

pages.text: In 2024, **Franco Colapinto** became the first Argentine in Formula 1 in 23 years. People got up at dawn on Sundays to watch him.
From 2009, the famous Dakar race left Africa and crossed Argentina for ten years. Millions of people stood by the road to watch it pass.

classes.title: The club on the corner
classes.summary: Who owns River, where kids spend the summer and a game with glass walls

pages.text: Every barrio has a **club**: a football field, a gym, a small bar and a room for parties. Children do sport there and old men play cards.

pages.prompt: Who is the owner of a giant club like River Plate?
pages.explain: Argentine clubs belong to their **socios**, the members, who pay every month and vote for the president. Boca and River too.

pages.text: In summer the club is **la pileta**, the swimming pool. Children go to the **colonia**: a day camp with games and swimming while parents work.
Old men play **bochas** there: heavy balls rolled along a long court, as close as possible to a small one. Italian immigrants brought the game.
The sport of the moment is **pádel**: tennis for four, in a small court with glass walls. Argentina fell in love with it in the 1980s, long before most of Europe.

pages.prompt: The Argentine **Fernando Belasteguín** was number one in the world at [pádel]. For how long?
pages.explain: Sixteen years in a row. For a long time almost every top player in the world was Argentine.

pages.text: The club bar has a **metegol**: football on a table, with players on metal bars. One rule everywhere: no spinning the bar. That's **molinete**, and the goal doesn't count.
Asking about sport is easy small talk. **“¿Hacés algún deporte?”** Do you do any sport? **“Juego al pádel los martes.”** I play [pádel] on Tuesdays.

sections.title: Animals
sections.summary: The carpincho and the birds you'll see every day

classes.title: The carpincho
classes.summary: The calm giant that took over a rich neighborhood

pages.text: The **carpincho**, or capybara, is the biggest rodent in the world, a relative of mice and guinea pigs. An adult can weigh more than 60 kilos, like a very big dog.
Carpinchos live in groups near rivers and lakes, in the warm northeast and in the wetlands around Buenos Aires. They eat grass and sleep a lot.

pages.prompt: In 2021, carpinchos were in the news all over the world. Why?
options: One swam across the river to Uruguay
They walked into a rich private barrio and stayed
They ate a whole field of yerba
pages.explain: **Nordelta**, a neighborhood of big houses, was built on the land where they lived. They came back, ate the gardens and crossed the streets. Most of the country was on their side.

pages.text: They are calm with everyone. Birds stand on their backs and other animals sit next to them. On the internet they're called the friendliest animal in the world.

pages.prompt: Carpinchos are very good at one sport. Which one?
pages.explain: Their feet are a bit like a duck's, and they can stay under water for minutes to hide from danger.

pages.text: The best place to see hundreds of them is the **Esteros del Iberá**, in Corrientes: a huge wetland full of birds, deer and **yacarés**, small relatives of the crocodile.
That's why a [carpincho] is your guide in this app. Calm, friendly, good with everyone, and very Argentine.

classes.title: The national bird
classes.summary: A small brown builder, loud green parrots and a bird that lies

pages.text: Argentina's national bird is not a great eagle. It's the **hornero**: small, brown, and living in every plaza and garden.

pages.prompt: **Hornero** comes from *horno*, oven. Why is the bird called that?
options: It builds a round nest of mud, like an old oven
It lives near kitchens and eats bread
Its chest is red like fire
pages.explain: A pair builds the nest from mud and straw in about two weeks: on a pole, a traffic light, a statue's head. It's a symbol of home and hard work.

pages.text: The noise in every park in Buenos Aires comes from **cotorras**: small green parrots. They build huge shared nests of sticks, high in the trees.
The **benteveo** has a yellow chest and shouts its own name. Many people hear something else in its call: **“¡bicho feo!”**, ugly bug.

pages.prompt: The **ñandú** is the big bird of the open country, as tall as a person. What can't it do?
pages.explain: It runs at up to 60 km/h but never leaves the ground. And the father sits on the eggs and raises the chicks, not the mother.

pages.text: The **tero** screams when you come near its nest. But it screams far from the eggs, to send you the wrong way.
So there's a saying for someone who talks about one thing to hide another: he's **como el tero**. He shouts in one place and has his eggs in another.

sections.title: Luck and beliefs
sections.summary: Saints of the road, the unlucky day and grandma's cures

classes.title: Red flags by the road
classes.summary: Gauchito Gil, the Difunta Correa and the saints the Church didn't choose

pages.text: Drive on any road in Argentina and you'll see them: small red houses, the size of a box, with red flags and candles around them.

pages.prompt: Who are those little red houses for?
options: A gaucho killed about 150 years ago
People who died in accidents on that road
A football club with a red shirt
pages.explain: **Gauchito Gil**, from Corrientes. He's a saint of the people: the Church never named him one, but millions ask him for help.

pages.text: The story: he ran from the army and took from the rich. Before he was killed, he told the soldier: “Your son is very sick. Pray in my name and he'll live.” The boy lived.
Drivers honk when they pass one, for a safe trip. People leave red ribbons, wine and cigarettes to say thanks.
Other roadside houses are surrounded by bottles of water. Those are for the **Difunta Correa**, a woman who, the story says, died of thirst crossing the desert of San Juan.

pages.prompt: The story says that when she was found, something amazing had happened. What?
options: Her baby was still alive, drinking her milk
A spring of water had opened next to her
pages.explain: So travelers leave water for her, so she is never thirsty again. Truck drivers are the ones who trust her most.

pages.text: Asking a saint for something with a promise in return is a **promesa**. **“Hice una promesa”** explains why your friend is walking 60 kilometers or has stopped eating sweets.

classes.title: Tuesday the 13th
classes.summary: The unlucky day and the small rules for good luck

pages.text: The unlucky day is not Friday the 13th. It's **martes 13**, Tuesday. The saying: **“Martes 13, no te cases ni te embarques.”** Don't get married and don't get on a boat.
Never pass the salt from hand to hand. Put it down on the table and let the other person pick it up. People say hand to hand brings a fight.

pages.prompt: At a café, where should you NOT leave your bag, if you believe in bad luck?
options: On the chair next to you
pages.explain: People say a bag or wallet on the floor makes the money go away. Many cafés even have small hooks under the table.

pages.text: Bad luck is **mala suerte** or **yeta**. To keep it away, people say **“toco madera”** and touch wood, the same as in English.
A red ribbon on a baby's wrist or on the mirror of a car is against **la envidia**: other people's envy, which is believed to bring harm.

pages.prompt: Many women get the same small present at Christmas, to wear on New Year's night for luck. What is it?
pages.explain: A pink **bombacha**. It has to be new and it has to be a present. In December the shop windows are full of them.

pages.text: And if a broom touches your feet while someone is sweeping, the old people say you will never get married.

classes.title: Cures from grandma
classes.summary: What to do when the doctor can't help, by the aunt who knows

pages.text: Ate too much and your stomach hurts for days? Doctors have other names for it. Grandmas call it **empacho**, and they know someone who cures it.

pages.prompt: How does that person check if you have [empacho]?
options: She looks at your tongue with a candle
She measures the distance to your stomach with a ribbon
She puts a warm plate on your belly
pages.explain: It's **curar con la cinta**. You hold one end of a ribbon on your stomach, and she measures it three times with her arm, elbow to hand. If the measure changes, you're **empachado**.

pages.text: The other method is **tirar el cuerito**: she pulls the skin on your lower back until it makes a small sound. Children hate it.
Then there's **mal de ojo**, the evil eye: a strong headache that comes, people say, from someone's envy. The cure uses a plate of water, drops of oil and secret words.

pages.prompt: The story says the secret words can only be taught on a special night. Which one?
options: The first full moon of the year
pages.explain: Most families say midnight on **Nochebuena**, usually from an older woman to a younger one in the family. Learned on any other day, people say, they don't work.

pages.text: People say the cure works from far away. You send your full name by WhatsApp, and an aunt in another city does the rest. Many people with university degrees do it.
Ask them if they believe, and they'll answer with two words: **por las dudas**. Just in case.

classes.title: Walking to Luján
classes.summary: A night on foot, promises to saints and a line for work

pages.text: Every October, hundreds of thousands of people walk about 60 kilometers from Buenos Aires to the town of **Luján**. They walk all night to reach its big church.

pages.prompt: The church holds a small statue of the Virgin Mary. The story says that in 1630 it chose to stay there. How?
options: It was found in the river after a flood
A white bird landed on it and stayed
The cart carrying it would not move until it was taken off
pages.explain: The animals pulling the cart didn't move until that one box was put on the ground. People decided she wanted to stay. Today she is the patron saint of Argentina.

pages.text: On August 7, the line outside the church of **San Cayetano**, in Buenos Aires, is many blocks long. He's the saint of bread and work. Some people sleep there for days.
All along the road to Luján, strangers give the walkers water, fruit and [mate] for free. Others wait at the side to rub tired feet.
Football has its promesas too. “If we win the cup, I'll walk to Luján.” After a big title, plenty of fans really do it.

pages.prompt: Most Argentines say they are Catholic. How many go to church every week?
pages.explain: For many, religion is family events more than Sunday mass: a baby's **bautismo** (baptism) and a child's **primera comunión** (first communion) are big parties with all the cousins.

pages.text: Argentina has the biggest Jewish community in Latin America, and millions of people with Syrian and Lebanese grandparents. Many came on the same boats, a century ago.

sections.title: TV, films and laughs
sections.summary: Red news screens, lunches on TV, cult films and the jokes

classes.title: On TV
classes.summary: A red screen, a lunch that started in 1968 and a famous question

pages.text: The news channel everyone knows by sight is **Crónica TV**. Its style is giant white letters on a red screen and loud march music, for any news, big or tiny.

pages.prompt: Which of these does Crónica really put on the screen in giant letters?
pages.explain: It counts the days to summer and to spring every year. The red screen with **ÚLTIMO MOMENTO**, breaking news, is now a classic joke image online.

pages.text: **Mirtha Legrand** has had lunch on TV since 1968. Famous people sit at her table, eat and answer her sharp questions. She was born in 1927 and was still on air at 99.
For thirty years, the biggest show was **Marcelo Tinelli**'s: jokes, hidden cameras and a dance contest with famous people. The next morning, everyone at work talked about it.
The other queen of TV is **Susana Giménez**, with decades of talk shows and phone games. The whole country knows her simply as Susana.

pages.prompt: A guest once told Susana that a dinosaur from Patagonia was coming to a show in the city. What did she ask, in a line every Argentine knows?
pages.explain: People tell it as one word: **“¿Vivo?”** She says it was a joke. Today people say it when someone asks a question with an obvious answer.

pages.text: When the president speaks on all channels at the same time, it's a **cadena nacional**. Your show stops, and half the country complains.

classes.title: Series that went around the world
classes.summary: Argentine novelas with fans in very far places

pages.text: A daily TV series is a **novela**. For years, Argentina made them for teenagers with songs and a band: **Chiquititas**, **Rebelde Way**, **Floricienta**, **Casi Ángeles**.

pages.prompt: The band from **Rebelde Way** filled big concert halls far from home. In which country?
pages.explain: Israeli teenagers learned Spanish from Argentine novelas. The same story was later made again in Mexico, India and other countries.

pages.text: The woman behind those shows is the producer **Cris Morena**. Many of today's Argentine actors and singers started as children in her novelas.
**Natalia Oreiro** was born in Uruguay and became a star in Argentina with the [novela] **Muñeca brava**. Then the series was sold to dozens of countries.

pages.prompt: In one country she is so loved that in 2021 she was made a citizen. Which one?
pages.explain: In 2019 she sang in 13 Russian cities, twenty years after the series ended.

pages.text: The series adults love most is **Los simuladores**: four men who solve people's problems with huge, clever lies. Argentines can repeat whole scenes.
Want to practice? Watch **El encargado**, a dark comedy about the man who runs a building in Buenos Aires. It's porteño Spanish at normal speed.

classes.title: Films everyone can repeat
classes.summary: The lines every family knows, and a street full of theaters

pages.text: Argentina makes a lot of films for its size, and two of them won the Oscar for best foreign film. But the ones people love are not always the ones with prizes.
The film every family knows is **Esperando la carroza**, from 1985: a loud family argues about who has to take care of the grandmother.

pages.prompt: In its most famous scene, a man cries about how poor his brother is. What did he see on the brother's table?
pages.explain: **“Tres empanadas”**, said with tears: three old empanadas for two people. He's not really sad, and he ate one himself. Argentines repeat it today when there's not enough of something.

pages.text: **Relatos salvajes**, from 2014, tells six short stories of normal people who lose control: in traffic, at a wedding, at a public office. Argentines saw themselves in it.

pages.prompt: You go to see an American film for adults in a cinema in Buenos Aires. How is it shown?
options: In English, with nothing to read
In English, with Spanish words on the screen
pages.explain: Most films for adults are **subtituladas**. Children's films are **dobladas**, with Spanish voices. Good news if you're learning: you can read along.

pages.text: Buenos Aires has around 300 theaters, more than almost any city in the world. On **Avenida Corrientes**, the shows start late and the pizza places wait for the crowd after.
**Nueve reinas**, from 2000: two small thieves, one day and one big trick. You never know who is lying to whom. Many people call it the best Argentine film.

classes.title: What makes Argentines laugh
classes.summary: Teasing, jokes about themselves and one day to be careful

pages.text: Among friends, teasing is love. If your new friends make fun of your accent or your team, you're part of the group. If they are very polite to you, worry.

pages.prompt: Argentines love to tell jokes about themselves. What are those jokes usually about?
pages.explain: A classic: “The best business? Buy an Argentine for what he's worth and sell him for what he says he's worth.” Told by Argentines, with pride.

pages.text: The most loved comedy group ever is **Les Luthiers**. For more than fifty years they played funny songs in elegant suits, on instruments they built from tins, tubes and bicycle parts.
On TV, **Diego Capusotto** makes fun of rock stars, politicians and [porteños] in short, absurd videos. People repeat the lines of his invented characters as if they were real.

pages.prompt: On December 28, be careful with what you read and what people tell you. Why?
options: It's the day for jokes and fake news
It's the day everybody tells the truth
It's the day old debts must be paid
pages.explain: It's the **Día de los Inocentes**. If you believe the lie, they say: **“¡Que la inocencia te valga!”** More or less: good luck with being so innocent.

pages.text: When something bad happens in the country, the jokes arrive in minutes. Laughing at a crisis is how people get through it.
There's a phrase for all of it: **“Argentina, no lo entenderías.”** Argentina, you wouldn't understand. People post it under any photo of something crazy and local.

classes.title: The radio is always on
classes.summary: Football told like a poem, and the new radio on YouTube

pages.text: In taxis, kitchens, shops and kioscos, the radio is on. Morning shows are like company: the same voices every day, for decades.
The person who tells a football game live is the **relator**. A good one talks fast, invents poems as he talks and holds a **“gooool”** for ten seconds.

pages.prompt: Some fans watch the game on TV in a special way. How?
options: With the TV sound off and the radio on
Standing up for the whole game
With the screen covered during penalties
pages.explain: They prefer their favorite relator on the radio. The voice and the picture don't always match, and nobody cares.

pages.text: The most famous radio moment: Maradona's second goal against England in 1986. The [relator] **Víctor Hugo Morales** cried and called him **barrilete cósmico**: a kite from space.
Young people listen in a new way: on **streaming**. Channels on YouTube make live radio with cameras, all day, and fill big concert halls with their fans.

pages.prompt: In 2025, a live stream had more viewers than many TV shows. What did it show?
options: A chess game between two ministers
A man walking from Ushuaia to the north
Scientists looking at the bottom of the sea
pages.explain: Argentine scientists sent a robot with a camera deep into the sea near Mar del Plata. People watched for hours and gave names to the animals, like a starfish with a big bottom.

pages.text: Radio is great practice for your ear. Put on a morning show while you make breakfast, and don't worry if you only understand half.

sections.title: Las provincias
sections.summary: Argentina beyond Buenos Aires, from the salt flats to the end of the world

classes.title: Buenos Aires is not Argentina
classes.summary: A huge country, 23 provinces with their own pride, and a map that reaches Antarctica

pages.text: Argentina is huge: roughly five times France. From **La Quiaca** on the Bolivian border down to **Ushuaia**, you get high desert, jungle, vineyards, the flat pampa and glaciers.
There are 23 **provincias**, plus the city of Buenos Aires. Each province has its own governor, constitution, police and flag.

pages.prompt: On the official map every Argentine kid learns at school, which province is the biggest?
pages.explain: School maps include the slice of **Antarctica** that Argentina claims, and it belongs to Tierra del Fuego. Leave the ice out and Buenos Aires wins.

pages.text: The classic way to get around is the **micro**, the long-distance bus. Twenty hours overnight in a **coche cama**, a seat that folds almost flat, is normal, though many people now fly.

pages.prompt: About how many Argentines live in and around the city of Buenos Aires?
pages.explain: One in three: about 15 million people in one metro area. The rest of this huge country is much emptier.

pages.text: Nearly every town throws a **Fiesta Nacional** of something it's proud of: the Poncho in Catamarca, the Sun in San Juan, even the **Salame Quintero** in Mercedes.
Meet someone from the provinces? Ask **“¿Y qué extrañás de allá?”**, what do you miss from back home. Then settle in for twenty minutes about the food, the family and the landscape.

classes.title: The Noroeste: Andes, coca and Pachamama
classes.summary: Salta, Jujuy and the most Andean corner of the country

pages.text: Fly two hours north of Buenos Aires and you land in the Andes. **Salta** and **Jujuy** are Andean Argentina: adobe villages, llamas, ponchos and Quechua words in everyday Spanish.
In the little town of **Purmamarca** stands the **Cerro de los Siete Colores**, a hill striped red, purple, ochre and green. No paint involved: just layers of different minerals.

pages.prompt: On a bus to Humahuaca, the man next to you has one cheek full of something and offers you leaves from a little bag. What's going on?
options: He's sharing coca leaves for the altitude
He's offering you tobacco to chew
He's selling a herbal tea he grows
pages.explain: Up here lots of people **coquean**: they keep a ball of coca leaves in their cheek for hours against altitude, cold and tiredness. Taking a few is fine. So is **no, gracias**. Just don't pack any to take home.

pages.text: Nobody is shocked: Argentine law says chewing coca leaves is not drug use. A few leaves in your cheek are a world away from cocaine, which is very much illegal.

Every **primero de agosto** (1 August) the Andes honor the **Pachamama**, Mother Earth. Families dig a hole and “feed” it with food, coca, **chicha** (corn beer) and wine, to thank her and ask for a good year.

pages.prompt: That same morning, all over Argentina, even in Buenos Aires, many people drink a little of something on an empty stomach. What?
options: Caña with rue, against winter's bad luck
Hot mate with salt, against the flu
Red wine with honey, for money
pages.explain: **Caña con ruda**: cane liquor with rue, a bitter herb, soaked in it. Three sips on 1 August keep away the illnesses and bad luck of August, or so they say. The custom is Guaraní, from the northeast, but it shares the date.

pages.text: Jujuy's carnival starts by digging up a cloth devil from a pile of stones: the **desentierro del diablo**. The whole town parties until he's buried again.

classes.title: Cuyo: wine, water and the siesta
classes.summary: Mendoza, Malbec and the highest mountain outside Asia

pages.text: **Cuyo** is Mendoza, San Juan and San Luis: dry land at the foot of the Andes. It barely rains. Yet Mendoza's streets are lined with huge, shady trees.

pages.prompt: How does a desert city keep all those trees alive?
options: Open ditches carry snowmelt to every street
They're desert trees that need no water
pages.explain: Water from the Andes runs through **acequias**, open channels along the curb. The system goes back to the **Huarpe** people, before the Spanish.

pages.text: Walking home at night, mind your step. Everyone falls into an acequia once, and the locals will laugh, kindly.
Mendoza makes most of Argentina's wine. Touring **bodegas** (wineries) by bike is a local classic. At dinner just order **un tinto**, a red: odds are it's Malbec.

pages.prompt: Malbec is Argentina's flagship grape. Where does it originally come from?
pages.explain: From southwest France. It struggled back home and found its real home here, in sun, altitude and dry air.

pages.text: The grape harvest ends with the **Fiesta de la Vendimia**, in early March: parades, a huge show in the hills, and a harvest queen chosen from the queens of the province's 18 departments.
About three hours west of the city, on the road to Chile, stands **Aconcagua**: almost 7,000 meters, the highest mountain outside Asia. You don't need to climb it: there's a viewpoint near the road.

In Buenos Aires the **siesta** is a weekend luxury. Here, as in most of the provinces, it's the schedule: shops shut after lunch and the streets go silent. Don't call anyone or ring a doorbell between 2 and 5.

classes.title: Córdoba: fernet, cuarteto and the tonada
classes.summary: The province that sings when it talks, parties hard and jokes about everything

pages.text: You'll hear a [cordobés] before you see one. The **tonada** stretches the syllable before the stressed one: **“cordoobés”**. [Porteños] love imitating it. Cordobeses love telling them they do it badly.
Córdoba's nickname is **La Docta**, the learned one. The Jesuits founded the country's oldest university here, and the city is still full of students from all over Argentina.

pages.prompt: In Italy, [fernet] is a bitter shot after dinner. How does Córdoba drink it?
options: With Coca-Cola, in a tall glass
pages.explain: **Fernet con coca**, lots of ice and a proper foam on top: the drink of every party. Bitter the first time, addictive by the third.

pages.text: Argentina drinks more [fernet] than any other country, and Córdoba leads the way: the province is said to drink around a third of it. Drink slowly.
Saturday night means a **baile de cuarteto**, Córdoba's own party music. Its biggest star is **La Mona Jiménez**. The crowd dances in a giant circle round the floor, and you just follow it.

pages.prompt: Up in Córdoba's hills, **Villa General Belgrano** throws Argentina's big Oktoberfest. Who helped make it a German town?
pages.explain: In 1939 the German warship **Graf Spee** was sunk by its own crew near Montevideo. The sailors were held in Argentina, and some stayed for good in this town, which German families had already founded.

pages.text: Cordobeses are famous for their humor. Their signature word is **culiao**. Vulgar and an insult when angry, between friends it means “dude”. Wait until they call *you* [culiao] before you try it.

classes.title: The Litoral: rivers, falls and chamamé
classes.summary: Iguazú, Guaraní, Rosario and a very loud yell

pages.text: **Litoral** means coast, but none of it touches the sea. Its coasts are the banks of huge rivers: the **Paraná** and the **Uruguay**.
Up in **Misiones** the soil is bright red and the air is thick and humid. In the jungle stand the stone ruins of **Jesuit missions**, where thousands of [Guaraní] once lived.

pages.prompt: Iguazú's falls sit on the border with Brazil. What share of them is on the Argentine side?
pages.explain: Roughly 80% of the falls are Argentine. Brazilians will point out that their side has the better wide view. Both are right. The star is the **Garganta del Diablo**, a huge horseshoe of water right on the border.

pages.text: On street corners and at bus stations, people sell warm **chipá**, small cheese breads made with cassava flour. In the heat, locals drink **tereré**: [mate] with ice-cold water or juice.
The northeast is [Guaraní] land, and you can hear it. In **Corrientes**, [Guaraní] is an official language next to Spanish. A kid there is a **gurí**, not a [pibe].
The [Litoral]'s music is **chamamé**: accordion, guitar, and couples dancing in a tight embrace. Every January, Corrientes throws a huge national [chamamé] festival.

pages.prompt: At a [chamamé] dance, the man next to you throws his head back and lets out a long, piercing scream. What's happening?
options: He's letting out a yell of joy
He's calling his friends over to dance
He's telling the band to play faster
pages.explain: It's a **sapucai**, a Guaraní yell of joy, grief or courage. Nobody expects you to do one. But if you try, go loud.

pages.text: **Rosario**, Argentina's third city, lives by the Paraná. Walk the riverfront and order a **liso**, a small glass of draft beer. Rosarinos will remind you that Messi was born here and the flag was first raised here, in 1812.

pages.prompt: Rosario is hundreds of kilometers from the sea. Where do rosarinos go to the beach on a hot Sunday?
options: A lagoon in the pampa nearby
pages.explain: Little boats cross the river to the islands opposite the city, with sand, trees and a grill. And there are river beaches right in town.

classes.title: Patagonia: ice, wind and Welsh tea
classes.summary: Glaciers, Welsh tea, chocolate and the end of the world

pages.text: **Patagonia** covers more than a quarter of Argentina, yet hardly anyone lives there. Steppe, lakes, mountains and a wind that never stops. The tourists are the ones chasing their hats.
Near **El Calafate**, the **Perito Moreno** glacier ends in a high wall of ice. Every few years the ice crossed the lake, blocked the water like a dam, then broke in a huge collapse shown on TV.

pages.prompt: For decades, what made the Perito Moreno famous among glaciers?
options: It wasn't shrinking, unlike most others
It was the fastest-growing in the world
Its ice was bright pink in summer
pages.explain: It stayed stable while others melted. Bad news: since 2019 it has been retreating fast, and scientists doubt it will block the lake again any time soon.

pages.text: Long before any settlers, this was the land of the **Tehuelche** and the **Mapuche**. Many names on the map come from their languages: **Nahuel Huapi**, **Neuquén**, **Chubut**.
In 1865 a small ship brought a group of **Welsh** settlers to the Chubut valley. Their towns, chapels and tea houses are still there.

pages.prompt: Why did those Welsh families sail all the way to Patagonia?
options: To dig for gold in the rivers
To escape a famine back home
pages.explain: At home, English was pushing Welsh aside. Here they could live, pray and teach in Welsh. Some families still speak it.

pages.text: In towns like **Gaiman**, a **té galés** is a meal, not a snack: pots of tea, scones, jams and **torta negra**, a dense fruit cake made to last the winter. Go hungry.

**Bariloche** looks like the Alps, with chocolate shops on every corner. It's also where teens go on their end-of-school trip, the **viaje de egresados**. Every adult has stories. Few will tell you all of them.
At the very bottom of the map, **Ushuaia** calls itself **el fin del mundo**, the end of the world. From here, ships leave for Antarctica.

pages.prompt: Ushuaia has a little steam train, the **Tren del Fin del Mundo**. What was it first built for?
options: Taking prisoners out to cut wood
Hauling gold down from the mines
pages.explain: Ushuaia grew up around a prison. The train carried inmates to the forest to cut timber. Today it carries tourists along the same valley.

sections.title: Íconos e inventos
sections.summary: Mafalda, Borges, the birome and a Pope from Flores

classes.title: Mafalda and her gang
classes.summary: The six-year-old who worried about the whole world

pages.text: **Mafalda** is a little girl with a big bow and bigger questions: world peace, the Beatles, and why grown-ups run things so badly. **Quino** drew her from 1964 to 1973.

pages.prompt: Mafalda was not created for a comic strip. What was she first drawn for?
options: A poster for a political party
pages.explain: Her name had to start with M, like **Mansfield**, a brand of home appliances. The ad never ran, so she got her own comic strip instead.

pages.text: Her mortal enemy? **La sopa**. Mafalda hates soup almost more than war. Lots of readers saw politics in that bowl: everything you're forced to swallow.
Her gang: **Manolito**, obsessed with money at his dad's shop. **Susanita**, who dreams only of a husband and kids. Dreamy **Felipe**. Tiny, political **Libertad**. Every Argentine knows a Susanita.
She's loved far beyond Argentina. In Italy, the novelist **Umberto Eco** introduced her first book and called her an angry little heroine who rejects the world as it is.

pages.prompt: Mafalda has a statue in Buenos Aires. Where?
options: On a bench, on the corner where Quino lived
Outside the Casa Rosada, on Plaza de Mayo
In the lobby of the Teatro Colón
pages.explain: In **San Telmo**, at Chile and Defensa, right by the building where Quino lived. There's always a line for a photo on the bench next to her.

pages.text: Quino died in 2020, one day after the anniversary of Mafalda's first strip. Fans filled her bench in San Telmo with flowers and notes.

classes.title: Comics, cartoons and snow
classes.summary: The first animated film ever, a bird with no wings, and El Eternauta

pages.text: Argentines call cartoons **dibujitos**. And this country made the world's first animated feature film, **El Apóstol**, in 1917: long before *Snow White*.

pages.prompt: What was [El Apóstol] about?
options: The president setting fire to Buenos Aires
A gaucho crossing the pampa on foot
A talking condor looking for its family
pages.explain: It mocked President Yrigoyen, who flies up to the gods and burns the city to clean out corruption. Sadly, the only copy burned in a studio fire, so nobody can watch it today.

pages.text: **Clemente** is a striped bird with no wings, drawn by **Caloi**. During the 1978 World Cup, he picked a fight with the country's most famous radio commentator.

pages.prompt: What was the fight about?
options: Whether fans should throw paper in the stadiums
Whether the dictator should hand out the cup
pages.explain: The commentator asked fans not to throw **papelitos**, bits of paper, so the country wouldn't look messy. Clemente said **“¡Tiren papelitos, muchachos!”** Throw them, boys! The stadiums ended up covered in paper.

pages.text: **El Eternauta** began as a comic in 1957. A deadly snowfall covers Buenos Aires, and anyone it touches dies. In 2025 Netflix made it a hit series with **Ricardo Darín**.
The hero isn't one man, it's the group. Its idea, made famous by the series, is **nadie se salva solo**: nobody is saved alone. It's quoted at marches and whenever a neighbor needs a hand.
Its writer, **Héctor Oesterheld**, was kidnapped by the dictatorship and never seen again. So were his four daughters. That's why the Eternauta's silhouette appears at human-rights marches.

classes.title: The writers
classes.summary: Borges, Cortázar, Alfonsina and the songs every kid sings

pages.text: The writer every Argentine likes to mention is **Jorge Luis Borges**: short, dizzying stories about labyrinths, mirrors and infinite libraries.

pages.prompt: Borges went almost blind. What job did he get around the same time?
options: Film critic for a big newspaper
Head of a school for painters
pages.explain: He called it an irony: all those books, and no eyes to read them. He kept writing by dictating.

pages.text: Borges was nominated for the Nobel again and again, and never won. He's said to have joked that not giving it to him had become a Scandinavian tradition.
**Alfonsina Storni** was a feminist poet of the 1920s. She took her own life in the sea at Mar del Plata, and the song **“Alfonsina y el mar”** keeps her alive.
**Julio Cortázar**'s novel **Rayuela**, Hopscotch, can be read straight through, or by jumping between chapters along a map he gives you. It made him an idol for students.

pages.prompt: **María Elena Walsh** wrote the songs every Argentine kid sings. Her most famous is about Manuelita. Who's Manuelita?
options: A turtle who travels to Paris
A cow who dreams of tango
A girl who talks to the moon
pages.explain: Parents who sang **“Manuelita vivía en Pehuajó…”** (Manuelita lived in Pehuajó) as kids now sing it to theirs, word for word. At a kids' party, the adults sing loudest.

classes.title: Inventions and Nobels
classes.summary: A Hungarian's pen, the first fingerprint case, a Nobel's sauce and a heart surgeon

pages.text: In Argentina a ballpoint pen is a **birome**. **László Bíró**, a Hungarian journalist, patented it here in the 1940s with his partner **Juan Jorge Meyne**. Bi-ró plus Me-yne: [birome].

pages.prompt: Who was the [birome]'s first big customer?
options: A chain of Buenos Aires banks
pages.explain: Unlike fountain pens, it didn't leak at high altitude. Argentina is so proud that Bíró's birthday is the **Día del Inventor**.

pages.text: In 1892, in the town of **Necochea**, a murder became the first in the world solved with a fingerprint. The system came from **Juan Vucetich**, a Croatian immigrant working for the La Plata police.
In 1914 a Buenos Aires doctor, **Luis Agote**, did one of the first transfusions with blood kept in a flask, not straight from the donor's arm. A pinch of sodium citrate stopped it from clotting.
Argentina has five Nobel prizes. **Luis Leloir** won chemistry for his work on how the body handles sugars.

pages.prompt: The story goes that young Leloir also invented something now found in every Argentine supermarket. What?
options: Salsa golf: mayo mixed with ketchup
Dulce de leche sold in a jar
pages.explain: At a golf club in Mar del Plata, so the legend says. Nobody can prove it, and everyone loves telling it.

pages.text: **René Favaloro** spent years as a country doctor in La Pampa. Then, in Cleveland, he helped pioneer the heart **bypass**, now used worldwide. Back home, he built one of the country's top heart hospitals.

classes.title: Modern icons
classes.summary: A Pope who rode the subte, the Generación Dorada, Vilas and two Oscars

pages.text: **Jorge Bergoglio** grew up in **Flores**, Buenos Aires, and as archbishop rode the [subte]. In 2013 he became **Pope Francis**, the first Pope from the Americas.

pages.prompt: Pope Francis was a card-carrying member of something very Argentine. What?
pages.explain: A paying **socio**, a club member, of San Lorenzo. He kept his membership as Pope.

pages.text: At home he divided people: many adored him, others disliked his politics. As Pope he never came back to visit, and people still argue about why. He died in 2025.

**Manu Ginóbili**, from **Bahía Blanca**, won four NBA titles with San Antonio and led the **Generación Dorada** to Olympic gold at Athens 2004, beating the USA on the way. For once, a football country stayed up to watch basketball.
In 1977 **Guillermo Vilas** had a magical tennis season and won almost everything. He made tennis popular in Argentina.

pages.prompt: So where did the official ranking put Vilas that year?
pages.explain: The computer kept him behind Jimmy Connors. Plenty of Argentines never accepted it, and a Netflix documentary reopened the fight.

pages.text: Argentina has two Oscars for foreign-language film: **La historia oficial** and **El secreto de sus ojos**. The second stars **Ricardo Darín**, the face of Argentine cinema.
A friend says **“¿Vemos una peli de Darín?”** Say yes. *Nueve reinas*, *Relatos salvajes*, *Argentina, 1985*: you're in safe hands.

sections.title: Historia: el nacimiento de un país
sections.summary: From the first peoples to the granary of the world: how Argentina came to be, up to 1930

classes.title: Before Buenos Aires
classes.summary: The first peoples, a silver dream, and a city founded twice

pages.text: Long before the Spanish, this land was full of peoples: **guaraníes** in the northeast, **diaguitas** in the northwest valleys, **tehuelches** in Patagonia, **querandíes** on the pampa. Argentines call them **pueblos originarios**.
Their descendants are still here. Today **12 de octubre** is no longer the “Día de la Raza” but the Day of Respect for Cultural Diversity.

pages.prompt: Buenos Aires means “good airs”. Where did the name really come from?
options: A Virgin that sailors prayed to
The mild climate the explorers found
A port town in southern Spain
pages.explain: Sailors prayed to **Santa María del Buen Ayre** for good winds. The city kept the “good airs” and dropped the rest.

pages.text: In 1536 **Pedro de Mendoza** founded that first **Buen Ayre** on the Río de la Plata. It went badly: hunger, disease and fights with the querandíes. The survivors gave up and left.

pages.prompt: So where did the Buenos Aires that lasted come from?
options: A new fleet sent from Spain
pages.explain: **Juan de Garay** came down the river from Asunción, in today's Paraguay, and founded the city again in 1580, this time for good.

pages.text: Even the country's name is a hope. **Argentina** comes from the Latin for silver: the Spanish dreamed of silver mountains here.
The silver was real, but far away in **Potosí**, in today's Bolivia. For two centuries Buenos Aires stayed a small, muddy port, famous mostly for smuggling.

classes.title: A viceroyalty and two British invasions
classes.summary: How a smuggling port became a capital, and threw out the British twice

pages.text: In 1776 Spain made Buenos Aires the capital of a huge **Virreinato**: today's Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia. Suddenly the smuggling port was a capital.

The viceroy ruled from the fort, where the [Casa Rosada] stands today. Across the square sat the **Cabildo**, the town council, the voice of the locals. Its white building with arches is still there, now a museum.

pages.prompt: Look closely at the [Cabildo] today. What happened to it?
options: It lost arches to make room for avenues
It was moved stone by stone from Córdoba
It was built as a church, then converted
pages.explain: The city cut it twice to open new avenues. It went from eleven arches down to five.

pages.text: In 1806 a British force sailed in and took Buenos Aires. Nobody expected it.

pages.prompt: The British march in. What does the Spanish viceroy do?
options: Flees the city with the treasury
Leads the defense street by street
Surrenders and swears loyalty to Britain
pages.explain: Viceroy Sobremonte ran away, and people never forgave him. The British caught the treasure in Luján anyway, and he ended up in Córdoba. The locals had to fight on their own.

pages.text: Locals organized under **Santiago de Liniers** and threw the British out. In 1807 the British came back, bigger. [Porteños] fought street by street, and won again. Argentines call the two attacks the **invasiones inglesas**.
The story every kid learns: neighbors poured boiling water and oil from the flat rooftops onto British soldiers. Some of it is polished legend. The street fighting was very real.
Two downtown streets remember it: **Reconquista** and **Defensa**. And [porteños] learned they could beat an empire without Spain. So why keep obeying a viceroy?

classes.title: May and July: the big dates
classes.summary: The Revolución de Mayo, independence in Tucumán, and the streets named after them

pages.text: In 1808 Napoleon invaded Spain and locked up its king. In Buenos Aires a big question landed: if there's no king, who's in charge here?
On **25 de mayo de 1810**, locals removed the viceroy and formed their own government, the **Primera Junta**. That's the **Revolución de Mayo**, and why the main square is **Plaza de Mayo**.

pages.prompt: Every school drawing of that day shows the crowd outside the [Cabildo] holding the same thing. What?
pages.explain: A sea of umbrellas, in the rain. Historians have doubts: umbrellas were a pricey import back then, so the picture is probably exaggerated.

pages.text: Not quite independence yet: the Junta still ruled in the Spanish king's name, at least on paper. The formal break came six years later, and the war with Spain went on even longer.

pages.prompt: Where was independence finally declared?
options: In a family house in Tucumán
In the Cabildo of Buenos Aires
pages.explain: Delegates from the provinces met in **San Miguel de Tucumán** and declared independence on **9 de julio de 1816**.

pages.text: The house was rebuilt around the original room and is now the **Casa Histórica**, a museum and the classic school trip. Almost every Argentine kid has a photo in front of its door.
Both days are **feriados**. People pin a light-blue-and-white **escarapela** to their chest, and schoolkids act out 1810 in colonial costume, with mustaches drawn on in burnt cork.
The dates are on the map too. **Avenida 9 de Julio** is the huge one with the [Obelisco], and almost every town has a street called [25 de Mayo].

classes.title: San Martín, Belgrano and the flag
classes.summary: The man who made the flag and the general who crossed the Andes

pages.text: **Manuel Belgrano** was a lawyer and economist who ended up a general. In 1812, by the river in **Rosario**, he raised a light blue and white flag. Buenos Aires wasn't thrilled: it looked too independent.
Kids learn the **celeste** and white come from the sky and its clouds. Some historians aren't so sure.

pages.prompt: What's the rival theory about the flag's colors?
options: They were the Spanish royal family's colors
They copied a British regiment's uniform
They came from the old Inca empire
pages.explain: Some argue celeste and white were colors of the Borbón royal house. Others say they come from the Virgin Mary's robe. Nobody can prove any of the stories.

pages.text: Belgrano gave nearly everything to the cause and died poor. The day he died, **20 de junio**, is now **Día de la Bandera**, Flag Day.
**José de San Martín** had a bold plan: beat Spain in Peru by going through Chile. In 1817, from **Mendoza**, he led an army over Andes passes more than 4,000 meters high.
With thousands of men, mules and horses, he crossed the **cordillera**, helped free Chile, then Peru. Argentines call him the **Padre de la Patria**.

pages.prompt: San Martín died in France. Where is he today?
pages.explain: His remains came home. His tomb in the **Catedral** on Plaza de Mayo is guarded by **Granaderos** in old blue uniforms, the regiment he founded. The day he died, **17 de agosto**, is a holiday too.

pages.text: Every town has a San Martín street, square or statue, usually on horseback. If you're lost, head for the plaza: he's probably in the middle.

classes.title: Unitarios, federales and gauchos
classes.summary: Decades of civil war, Rosas, and the horsemen of the pampa

pages.text: Winning independence was one thing. Agreeing on how to run the country was harder: decades of civil war followed. **Unitarios** wanted one strong government in Buenos Aires. **Federales** wanted the provinces to rule themselves, each under its own **caudillo**.
Behind it all: who keeps the money from the port? Buenos Aires had a clear answer: Buenos Aires.
**Juan Manuel de Rosas**, a rich landowner and a federal, ran Buenos Aires from 1829 to 1852, with one short break, and with near-total power.

pages.prompt: Under Rosas, one color was all but required. Which?
pages.explain: Wearing federal red was the safe choice. His enforcers, the **Mazorca**, terrorized anyone who looked like an opponent.

pages.text: Argentines still argue about him. A bloody tyrant, said liberals like **Sarmiento**, a writer and later president. A defender of the country against British and French fleets, say others. Don't raise it at an [asado] unless you have time.
Out on the pampa lived the **gauchos**: expert horsemen who worked cattle, with knife, poncho, [mate] and guitar. Governments treated them as vagrants and forced many into the army.

pages.prompt: So what turned the gaucho into a national hero?
options: A long poem about one of them
A tango about life on the pampa
pages.explain: **Martín Fierro** (1872), by **José Hernández**, tells of a gaucho dragged to the frontier who ends up an outlaw. Most kids meet it at school.

pages.text: Hernández's birthday, **10 de noviembre**, is the **Día de la Tradición**. Towns like **San Antonio de Areco** fill with horses, ponchos and folk music.
The most quoted lines: **“Los hermanos sean unidos, porque esa es la ley primera.”** Brothers, stick together. Argentines still say it, usually in the middle of a family fight.

classes.title: The Campaña del Desierto
classes.summary: A plan to fill the country, and a war over land still argued about

pages.text: After Rosas fell in 1852, a **Constitución** was written in 1853. The new leaders' motto: **gobernar es poblar**, to govern is to populate. Bring immigrants, railways and money.

And schools. **Domingo Faustino Sarmiento**, president from 1868, opened them all over the country, and an 1884 law made primary school free and compulsory. The day he died, **11 de septiembre**, is **Día del Maestro**, Teachers' Day.

The plan also meant taking land. Between 1878 and 1885, the army, first led by **Julio Argentino Roca**, took the pampa and Patagonia from the **mapuches**, **ranqueles**, **tehuelches** and other peoples.

pages.prompt: Official history called it the **Conquista del Desierto** or Campaña del Desierto: the conquest of the desert. Why “desert”?
options: It painted a lived-in land as empty
The land was mostly sand dunes
pages.explain: Those lands were home to whole peoples. Calling them “desert” made taking them sound like settling nothing.

pages.text: By the army's own count for 1879, over a thousand people were killed and over ten thousand taken prisoner. Families were split up and many forced to work as servants. The land went to a few big owners.
For a long time schools taught it as a heroic conquest. Today many historians and indigenous communities call it a **genocidio**. Others reject that word. Many now write the name in quotes.
Roca was on the old 100-peso bill, and his statues stand in many towns. Who should be on banknotes and statues is part of the same argument.

pages.prompt: In a town square you see a statue of Roca. What's likely to have happened to it lately?
options: Splashed with red paint, then cleaned again
Moved indoors to a history museum
Covered in flowers every Día de la Tradición
pages.explain: His statues get painted, cleaned and painted again. Some want them gone, others want them kept. It's the same debate, in the street.

classes.title: The boats: immigrants and conventillos
classes.summary: Millions of Europeans, one room per family, and the mix that made Buenos Aires

pages.text: From the 1870s on, ships brought millions of Europeans, mostly **italianos** and **españoles**. For a while, around half of Buenos Aires was born abroad.
Hence the old joke: Mexicans descend from the Aztecs, Peruvians from the Incas, and Argentines… **from the boats**. It forgets the indigenous and Afro-Argentine people who were already here.

pages.prompt: In Buenos Aires, what nickname does a man from Madrid often get?
pages.explain: Galicia sent so many people that **gallego** came to mean any Spaniard. Italians are **tanos**. In the same way, Arabs were called **turcos** and Jews **rusos**, whatever country they came from. Among friends these are usually friendly.

pages.text: New arrivals could sleep free for a few days at the **Hotel de Inmigrantes**, by the port, while they looked for work. Today it's a museum, and people search its records for their great-grandparents.
Many ended up in **conventillos**: old houses split into single rooms, one family per room, one patio and bathroom for dozens. Italians, Spaniards, Jews, Arabs and locals, all together.

pages.prompt: In 1907, tenants all over Buenos Aires went on a rent strike. What did women and kids march with?
pages.explain: Brooms, to “sweep away” the landlords. That patio life, with its fights and its songs, fed the city's slang and its tango.

pages.text: The boats still matter. For decades, Argentines hunted down a grandparent's or great-grandparent's papers to get an Italian or Spanish passport. Italy made its rules stricter in 2025, but a great many Argentines already have one.

classes.title: The granary of the world
classes.summary: Trains, wheat, the secret vote, rooftop radio, and the coup that ended it all

pages.text: Around 1900 Argentina shipped wheat, corn and beef across the ocean, mostly to Britain. It proudly called itself **el granero del mundo**: the world's granary.
British money built the railways. Look at the map: the lines spread out from Buenos Aires like an open fan, all carrying grain and cattle to one port.
Around the 1910 centenary, many felt they lived in one of the richest countries on earth. The **Teatro Colón** opened. But the best land sat in a few hands.

pages.prompt: It's 1905 and you walk into a polling station. How do you vote?
options: Out loud, in front of everyone
By raising your hand in a hall
pages.explain: The **voto cantado**, the sung vote: you said your choice aloud, with the local boss listening. Fraud was routine.

pages.text: In 1912 the **Ley Sáenz Peña** made voting secret and compulsory for men. That's why voting is still compulsory in Argentina today. Women had to wait until 1947.
In 1916 the first presidential election under the new law was won by **Hipólito Yrigoyen**. He led the **radicales** (the UCR party), still one of the main parties today.

pages.prompt: In 1920, four friends climbed onto a theater roof in Buenos Aires. What did they do up there?
pages.explain: They broadcast Wagner's *Parsifal* to a few dozen homemade radio sets: one of the world's first public broadcasts. They're remembered as **los locos de la azotea**, the rooftop madmen.

pages.text: Then came the 1929 crash, and grain and beef prices sank. In 1930 the army overthrew President **Yrigoyen**: the first of many coups, and the end of the granary years.

sections.title: Historia: el siglo XX y hoy
sections.summary: Perón, the dictatorship, Malvinas, 2001 and why everyone thinks in dollars

classes.title: Coups, Perón and Evita
classes.summary: The man who still splits family asados, and the woman millions mourned

pages.text: From 1930 to 1983, the army overthrew governments again and again. The good news: since 1983 Argentina has had its longest run of democracy ever, and most Argentines guard it fiercely.

**Juan Domingo Perón** was a colonel in the government of the 1943 coup. As labor secretary he backed the unions: pensions, paid holidays, labor courts. Many workers felt they finally had a friend up high.

pages.prompt: In 1945 Perón's rivals forced him out and locked him up on an island. What got him out?
options: A secret deal with the navy
A ruling from the Supreme Court
pages.explain: On **17 de octubre**, workers from the factory suburbs filled **Plaza de Mayo** and demanded him back. Some cooled their tired feet in the fountains, an image that became legend.

pages.text: That night Perón spoke from the balcony of the [Casa Rosada]. Peronists still celebrate 17 October as the **Día de la Lealtad**, Loyalty Day. In 1946 he was elected president, and re-elected in 1951.

**Evita**, a young actress from a small town, married Perón. Her foundation built hospitals and schools, and she pushed the 1947 law that gave women the vote. She died in 1952, aged 33. Millions queued for days to say goodbye.
Opponents mocked Perón's supporters as **descamisados**, the shirtless ones. Perón and Evita turned the insult into a badge of pride.

pages.prompt: Peronists have an animal nickname for anti-Peronists. Which animal?
pages.explain: **Gorila**. It's an insult, so don't use it unless you know the people well. Anti-Peronists have their own names for Peronists, too.

pages.text: In 1955 a coup threw Perón out, and Peronism was banned for almost two decades. He came back in 1973, won a third time and died in office in 1974. His widow and vice-president, **Isabel Perón**, took over.
Argentines still disagree about him. Supporters remember workers' rights, dignity and the vote for women. Critics remember jailed opponents, a controlled press and a cult of the leader.

Today the political divide is called **la grieta**, the crack. The word is from the 2010s, about the Kirchner governments and their opponents, but the split is much older. Many families ban politics at Sunday lunch. Respect it.

classes.title: The last dictatorship
classes.summary: 1976–1983: the disappeared, the Madres and Abuelas, and “Nunca más”

pages.text: On **24 de marzo de 1976** a military junta led by **Jorge Rafael Videla** overthrew President Isabel Perón. The country was in crisis: guerrilla attacks, right-wing death squads, very high inflation. What followed was far worse.

The regime hunted anyone it called “subversive”: guerrillas, but also union delegates, students, lawyers, teenagers. People were kidnapped, taken to secret centers like the **ESMA**, tortured, and thousands were murdered.

Families got no body and no answer. The victims are **los desaparecidos**, the disappeared. In 1984 the **CONADEP** commission documented about 9,000 cases. Human rights groups speak of 30,000. The regime hid its records, and the number is still disputed.

pages.prompt: In 1977, mothers of the disappeared met in [Plaza de Mayo]. Gatherings were banned, and police told them to move along. What did they do?
options: Kept walking in pairs around the monument
Moved their meetings into a church nearby
Went home and wrote letters abroad
pages.explain: Standing still was a gathering. Walking wasn't. So they walked in circles around the monument. The white headscarf came a few months later: at first it was a baby's cloth diaper.

pages.text: They're the **Madres de Plaza de Mayo**, and the walk still happens every Thursday afternoon, now with the last few Madres and many supporters. Their white **pañuelo** is painted on the ground around the square's monument.

Babies born to prisoners were handed to other families under false names. The **Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo**, the grandmothers, think there were about 500. They have searched for them ever since, and found about 140.

pages.prompt: With the parents gone, how could the Abuelas prove a young person was their grandchild?
options: A DNA test using the grandparents' blood
Birth records kept secretly by nurses
pages.explain: They helped push scientists to create a “grandparent” DNA test. Each **nieto restituido**, a grandchild who gets their identity back, makes national news.

pages.text: In 1985 civilian judges put the junta leaders on trial: the **Juicio a las Juntas**. Prosecutor **Julio Strassera** closed with **“Señores jueces: nunca más.”** Videla got life. The film *Argentina, 1985* tells that story.

It didn't end there. Laws from 1986–87 stopped most other trials, and in 1989–90 President Menem pardoned those convicted. In the 2000s the laws were struck down and trials began again. Over a thousand people have been convicted.
Every 24 March, the **Día de la Memoria**, hundreds of thousands march to [Plaza de Mayo] with photos of the disappeared: **Memoria, Verdad y Justicia**.

classes.title: Malvinas
classes.summary: The 1982 war, the young soldiers, and a claim nearly every Argentine shares

pages.text: The **Islas Malvinas** sit in the South Atlantic, off Patagonia. Britain has held them since 1833 and Argentina has claimed them ever since. The British call them the Falkland Islands. Here, always say **Malvinas**, never Falklands.
In 1982 the dictatorship faced a collapsing economy and growing protests. On **2 de abril** its troops landed on the islands, and crowds cheered in [Plaza de Mayo]. Britain sent a fleet.

pages.prompt: Who made up most of Argentina's troops on the islands?
options: Career soldiers with years of training
Volunteers who signed up after the landing
pages.explain: Most were **conscriptos** of 18 to 20, barely out of school. Argentines call them **los chicos de la guerra**, the kids of the war. They were sent to freezing trenches, often underfed and badly equipped.

pages.text: 649 Argentines died. Almost half of them went down with one ship, the cruiser **General Belgrano**.

pages.prompt: During the war, what did most people at home hear from the news?
pages.explain: Censored news and magazines kept saying **“estamos ganando”**, we're winning, almost until the surrender in June. The shock turned into fury. General **Galtieri**, the head of the junta, was out within days, and the weakened regime had to call elections. Democracy came back in 1983.

pages.text: Today 2 April is a national holiday for the **ex combatientes** and **los caídos**, the veterans and the fallen. For years many veterans felt forgotten, and the wounds are still an open subject.

You'll see **“Las Malvinas son argentinas”** on road signs, murals and buses. The claim is one of the few things almost everyone agrees on. The war is different: most see it as a reckless bet by the dictatorship.
If it comes up, listen more than you argue. Plenty of Argentines have a relative or neighbor who fought there.

classes.title: Democracy, hyperinflation and 2001
classes.summary: From Alfonsín to “que se vayan todos”

pages.text: In 1983 democracy returned with **Raúl Alfonsín**. His promise is still quoted: **“con la democracia se come, se cura y se educa”**. With democracy, people eat, heal and learn.
The economy didn't cooperate. By 1989 prices went wild: inflation passed 3,000% in that one year. Supermarkets relabeled prices several times a day.

pages.prompt: It's 1989 and you just got paid. What's the smart move?
options: Spend it all that same day
Put it in a savings account
Keep it at home for next month
pages.explain: Money lost value in your pocket by the hour. People ran to the supermarket on payday, a reflex some Argentines still have.

pages.text: In 1991, under President **Carlos Menem**, a Peronist, a law tied the currency to the dollar: soon **one peso = one dollar**, the **convertibilidad**. Inflation fell to almost zero. Imports and trips abroad got cheap, and state companies were sold.
The bill came later: factories closed, unemployment passed 18%, and the country borrowed more and more to keep one peso equal to one dollar. Argentines still argue about that decade.
December 2001: people rushed to pull out their savings, so the government capped withdrawals. That's the **corralito**. The middle class went out to the streets banging pots: the **cacerolazo**.

pages.prompt: On 20 December President De la Rúa resigned and left the [Casa Rosada] by helicopter. Counting him, how many presidents did Argentina have in about twelve days?
pages.explain: Five: De la Rúa, Puerta, Rodríguez Saá, Camaño and Duhalde. The first resigned, the next three lasted only days, and Duhalde stayed until 2003. The chant on every street was **“¡Que se vayan todos!”**: out with all of them.

pages.text: Those days were violent too. On 19 December shops were looted and the government declared a state of siege. People went out anyway. In two days, 39 people were killed across the country, in the looting and the police repression.

In 2002 the one-to-one peso ended. Dollar savings were turned into pesos by force, and more than half the country fell below the poverty line. A whole generation learned never to fully trust a bank again.

classes.title: From 2003 to today
classes.summary: Kirchner, Macri, Fernández, Milei, and how to stay out of the argument

pages.text: In 2003 a Peronist governor from Patagonia, **Néstor Kirchner**, became president. His wife, **Cristina Fernández de Kirchner**, followed him from 2007 to 2015. Their movement is **kirchnerismo**. In headlines, they're **los K**.

Supporters remember jobs and wages coming back, wider pensions and child benefits, and new trials for the dictatorship's crimes. Critics point to rising inflation, official statistics few people trusted, currency controls and corruption cases.

pages.prompt: In 2015 the country voted for change and elected **Mauricio Macri**. What had he run before he ran the country?
options: A late-night talk show on TV
pages.explain: Macri, a businessman, was president of Boca and then mayor of Buenos Aires. He governed from 2015 to 2019.

pages.text: Supporters of Macri value statistics people could trust again, more open trade and new roads and public works. Critics point to a record loan from the IMF, and to inflation and poverty that were higher when he left.

In 2019 Peronism returned with **Alberto Fernández** (2019–2023), and Cristina Kirchner as vice-president. Then came the pandemic. Supporters value the emergency aid and the vaccines. Critics point to a very long lockdown and inflation that passed 200% a year.

pages.prompt: In the 2023 campaign, the economist **Javier Milei** carried one object at his rallies. Which one?
pages.explain: **La motosierra**, the chainsaw, was his picture of what he would do to state spending. Milei calls himself a **libertario**, a libertarian. He has been president since December 2023.

pages.text: Supporters of Milei point to much lower inflation, a state that no longer spends more than it earns, and fewer currency controls. Critics point to cuts in pensions, universities and public works, and a hard first year for many families.
The divide between the two camps is **la grieta**, the crack, and it runs through families and groups of friends. Whoever governs, two subjects never leave the table: prices and the dollar.
As a visitor, you don't need to pick a side. Ask **“¿Vos qué pensás?”** What do you think? Then listen. You'll learn a lot.

classes.title: Money today: thinking in dollars
classes.summary: Inflation, the dólar blue, arbolitos and cash under the mattress

pages.text: After all that, Argentines live by one rule: pesos to spend, dollars to save. Plenty of savings sit at home in cash, **bajo el colchón**, under the mattress.

pages.prompt: You're buying an apartment in Palermo. How is it usually paid for?
options: In US dollars, often counted in cash
pages.explain: Apartments are priced in dollars (**U$S**), and it's common for the notes to be counted on the spot at signing.

pages.text: Inflation even ate the money itself. Your Argentine grandparents may have used five different currencies, each one born by chopping zeros off the last.

For years buying dollars was capped (the **cepo**), so a parallel market grew: the **dólar blue**. At one point there were over a dozen dollar rates, even a **dólar Coldplay** for paying foreign bands to come and play.

pages.prompt: On [calle] Florida, a man keeps muttering “Cambio, cambio.” Locals call him an **arbolito**, a little tree. Why, the story goes?
options: He stands in the same spot all day, like a tree
He hides behind street trees from the police
The first ones worked out of a city park
pages.explain: The usual story: he stands planted on the sidewalk all day, and his “leaves” are green, like dollar bills. He's a street money changer. He'll walk you to a **cueva**, a “cave”: the back office where the swap happens. It's unofficial, and fake notes are a real risk.

pages.text: In 2025 the cap on buying dollars was lifted for ordinary people. The habit stays: **¿A cuánto está el dólar?** is small talk, like the weather.
Before you pay, ask. Many shops give a discount for **efectivo** (cash) or transfer. When they ask **“¿Efectivo o tarjeta?”**, the answer can change the price.
